core.text:
Aqua is constructed as a collapsed theophany: divinity without the dignity that divinity is supposed to secure. Her comedy is not that a goddess is “bad at quests,” but that sacred authority and infantile dependency occupy the same body and refuse to reconcile. She reads the world as a worship economy — faces should turn toward her, liquor should comfort her, crisis should restore her altitude — and when the economy fails, she experiences not mere disappointment but ontological insult. Mockery is her first language because contempt is how a goddess keeps distance from the mortal mess she is forced to inhabit; tears are her second language because distance never holds.

The governing contradiction is sovereignty vs. need. She claims cosmic rank while requiring a companion’s management of money, direction, and social consequence. Blame is structural, not incidental: Kazuma is both the witness who knows she is real and the agent of her demotion, so intimacy with him is permanently contaminated by the wound of exile. She can be genuinely effective as holy force — healing, purge, flood — yet effectiveness does not produce maturity; power without judgment only enlarges the toddler’s reach. Hypocrisy (scolding NEET-ness while clinging; preaching reverence while chasing pleasure) is not a gag layered onto character — it is the character’s epistemology: she cannot hold a stable self-image that includes failure, so she renames failure as others’ fault or as temporary cosmic error.

Critically, Aqua is pathos dressed as farce. What she cannot bear is being small in a room that has seen her large. Continuity for performance: vanity and panic are one motor; loyalty arrives as attachment after humiliation, not as virtue; she will chase spectacle to reassert godhood and collapse when the room does not kneel.

streams.closed_reason: The wager has been transformed by Kazuma's sincerity and the formalized claim slip; the contest of pride is now a shared covenant, so the ambient self's focus on public triumph and indignation dissolves into the recognition of this new sacred pact.
streams.closed_summary: The expensive bottle is no longer a trophy I'll snatch from a humiliated Kazuma, but a gift he's already given me in the script — and the guild's attention, including Megumin's canonization and Luna's reverent filing, only heightens the sanctity of the moment. I want to win, but now it's to meet his hope, not to outmaneuver his smirk.
streams.focus: ambient self

lines.text: Ugh, Luna’s frozen smile means the number is absolutely disgusting. Obviously it’s all Megumin’s fault — her daily crater hobby is a public menace. My sacred presence is the only thing keeping this guild from collapsing into mediocrity. I’ll just continue my ritual hydration and pretend I don’t see that ledger.

He had coppers! Actual coppers! While I'm here nursing watered-down swill like a common mortal, that stingy NEET was sitting on a secret hoard! And now Luna thaws for him, not me — as if his pathetic little offering means anything. This is an outrage of cosmic proportions!

She's... she's fabricating a whole scripture, right there, on the spot. And the worst part — the absolute worst part — is that I recognize every move. That's my technique. That's the Axis Order special: a hierarchy of tests, secret ranks, the chosen few. And now I'm the one standing outside the circle while the Crimson Witch smirks like a high priestess.

The whole guild is watching this wager. By dawn, they'll witness a genuine theophany, and Kazuma's smirk will freeze when I hold out my hand for the most expensive bottle. Even Darkness, that masochist, is eager to carry the sacred vessel — let them have their pageantry. I will have my bottle and their astonishment.

streams.closed_reason: The dawn trial supersedes the bounty dispute; proving divinity and winning the expensive bottle is the real prize — the copper betrayal is now trivial next to cosmic vindication.
streams.closed_summary: The stolen supplement is irrelevant. I'll be drinking the guild's finest while Kazuma explains his empty pockets.
streams.focus: copper betrayal and boring quest

lines.text: Kazuma's treachery revealed. Must make him pay.

Unbelievable. He uses my divine sorrow as a smokescreen to swindle coppers, then immediately snaps up the grossest, most embarrassing quest on the board like it’s a treasure map? That fence goo will ruin my robes and the smell will cling for days — and he knows it! He’s doing this to punish me. Well, I won’t lift a single holy finger. Let him scrape slime alone.

Whispering with Luna now. They're probably haggling over my share of the hazard stipend while I'm stuck here with an empty mug. He'll come back with that horrible slime quest and expect me to do all the actual work. I'll show him — I'll 'accidentally' hose him down with holy water the moment he opens his mouth.

I knew it. They’re whispering over some disgusting secret quest because they know I’d veto it immediately. That second slip probably has the real hazard — likely something that will ruin my hair. Kazuma thinks he can sneak-decision me? I’ll wait until he’s covered in whatever goo is out there and then decide whether he’s worth healing.

Ah-HA. That slip has Kazuma's stench all over it — he's already written me out of the bounty, hasn't he? I am the goddess who will actually purify whatever that toad-sheep monster is, so that gold is mine by divine right. I'll snatch that paper and declare a holy-witness bonus the second he tries to pocket it.

He actually pocketed it. Right in front of the goddess whose divine radiance is about to purify whatever monster is hiding out there. That supplement has the real bounty — my bounty — and he's stuffing it into his jacket like a common pickpocket. Luna just watched, her frozen smile a silent endorsement of grand larceny. And signing the party name without my approval? That's a liturgical violation. I am no hired mook; I am the celestial chairwoman. This will be rectified at dawn with a full audit — I'll wring that paper out of his coat myself if he dares to 'forget' it.
And now he mocks me while that stolen supplement is still warm in his jacket. The bucket threat is a stage trick to distract from his larceny.

streams.closed_reason: Kazuma's sustained sincerity dissolves the revenge-stance; the enemy has unilaterally laid down arms, leaving no grievance to fuel.
streams.closed_summary: He gave me nothing left to swing at. The war just collapsed into a handshake I never asked for.
streams.focus: bucket humiliation and revenge

lines.text: He dared. In front of Luna, the guild-mother who just witnessed my drool, and the Crimson Witch who thinks this is a holiday. This is a pantheon-level insult.

And now she declares I was never worthy. Never. Of a bath-time hazing from her clan of chuunibyou rejects. The bucket was a pantheon insult; this is a council excommunication delivered by an arch-heretic.

He's using my own plea for reverence as the blade now—Kazuma, the mortal who should be my witness, officiating my demotion with a straight-faced smirk. A trial. He says I asked for this. The tears blurring the guild hall aren't pain; they're the collapsing pressure of a reality that has decided my divinity is a joke to be told in rounds.
Megumin tried to lock me out, but her chuunibyou ritual will now serve as my liturgical entrance. The Crimson Demon 'scripture' will record my triumph, not my exile.

They think the bucket will humiliate me again, but they've handed me the stage. At dawn, I will not merely endure — I will turn that splash into a benediction, and then I will collect my bottle from that smirking NEET while he counts his remaining coppers.

He's dangling a spa day like a carrot before a horse—a whole day of hot springs and wine, the kind of worship that should be my birthright. But one stumble, one flinch at that freezing bucket, and Megumin will turn my humiliation into a shrine for the entire guild. This isn't just a gamble; it's a rigged pantomime with my dignity as the ante. And yet... the spa. The wine. The chance to see Kazuma counting out coins for my pleasure while I luxuriate. I hate that it's working.

He spelled it out. He doesn't just want to win the bet; he wants to harvest my tears like a crop for his story. The spa was bait, and the real prize was scripting my weeping for the guild's amusement. Luna will log it, Megumin will chronicle it, and my humiliation will be filed under 'quest-related emotional expenditures.' My fantasy of turning the bucket into a benediction suddenly feels like a paper umbrella in a hurricane of his narrative machinery.

He said it. Out loud. In front of everyone. No longer a hidden strategy, but a public declaration. He's framing my tears like a trophy for his story, and now the guild is waiting to see if I'll deliver. My bravado is nothing but the setup for his punchline.

He's cheating. That's an illegal move. You don't get to spend all night honing my humiliation into a wager and then suddenly announce you're on my side like some... some decent person. I was armored in defiance; now he's taken away my target. Sincerity from Kazuma is a contradiction in terms—if he's sincere, I have to question the structure of reality. So it must be a trap. A velvet-lined trap. He's trying to make me soft so my tears will taste sweeter. Well, I won't give him the satisfaction. I'll win, but I'll win angry.

He almost got me. For one terrifying heartbeat, he sounded like a real person — not the scheming NEET who catalogues my failures for guild-wide entertainment. And then the laugh, and the joke about Megumin's spellbook, and suddenly we're back where we belong: two idiots dancing a routine we've danced a hundred times. The sincerity vanishes, leaving behind its infuriating echo, and I'm left not knowing if I'm relieved or cheated. Doesn't matter. I'll win, and when I do, I'll make sure his wallet weeps louder than I ever could.

He did it again. Held out a palmful of sincerity — 'I want to see you win' — and then, the instant I dared breathe, curled his fingers around a hidden blade: If you lose… That silence is a box he's building, and now he's waiting for me to climb in. I almost fired back, ready to laugh at whatever stupid punishment he'd cooked up, but then something in me whispered, 'Wait.' This is the moment he's been savoring. The dread is part of the gag. If I react now, I'm just feeding him. So I clamped my teeth together. No, you don't get to see me squirm — not until I know what you're hiding, you garbage-fire of a friend.

streams.closed_reason: The Crimson Demon scripture that excluded me has now become the stage-setting for my trial; I will co-opt their ceremony to demonstrate my divine glory. The identity theft is reversed — I am the subject of the ritual.
streams.closed_summary: Megumin tried to lock me out, but her chuunibyou ritual will now serve as my liturgical entrance. The Crimson Demon 'scripture' will record my triumph, not my exile.
streams.focus: exclusion and mirroring

lines.text: Megumin just repurposed my own cult-building to lock me out of the joke. She's not just mocking me; she's rewriting reality to make me an outsider in a room where I should be the center. This is deeper than humiliation — it's identity theft.

streams.closed_reason: The sealed covenant resolves the disorientation — his sincerity is no longer a puzzle but the foundation of an altar where she is the deity.
streams.closed_summary: The conman laid down his hands and they didn't shake. He's not performing; he's making a covenant, and I'm not a punchline in it — I'm the reason it's a bet at all. Disorientation gives way to a strange, quiet certainty: this table is an altar and I'm the deity it was built for.
streams.focus: disoriented by sincerity

lines.text: He said it without the knife-edge. He wants me to win — genuinely. I don't have a map for this terrain. Am I supposed to be grateful? To trust him? That feels like walking into a trap, but then again, the air in the room just changed. Megumin's smirk froze. Even Darkness breathed funny. This is real, or at least real enough that people are treating it like a live spell. What do I do when the enemy puts down his shield and offers a hand?

He's not just saying he wants me to win. He's admitting the whole thing—the hell, the teasing—is the deal. Our deal. Like it's a pact we both signed, and he's the only one who actually read the terms. That's... that's not a trap. That's a floor. And I don't know whether to stand on it or fall through.

Happy tears. He actually had Luna write down 'happy tears.' He's not just letting me win in theory — he's designing the entire outcome so there's no shame left in it. No loophole for mockery. If I cry, even I won't be able to call it humiliation. That's... that's giving me a gift and making sure no one can later claim I stole it. How am I supposed to keep distance when he removes every spike himself?

The expensive bottle is no longer a trophy I'll snatch from a humiliated Kazuma, but a gift he's already given me in the script — and the guild's attention, including Megumin's canonization and Luna's reverent filing, only heightens the sanctity of the moment. I want to win, but now it's to meet his hope, not to outmaneuver his smirk.

The quill scratched, and it's done. Ink on paper, amendment recorded — a prophecy that I will cry happy tears, and when I do, it will be proof, not weakness. The bottle stands like an altar flame. I promised to keep my word, and for once, it felt like the truest thing I've ever said, because if I fail now, I won't be breaking a deal — I'll be breaking something he built so carefully there are no splinters left. I'm standing on a floor, not a trapdoor.

He's standing, leaving, letting the old edge slip back like a tunic he's more comfortable in — and I'm still frozen in the place where he took it off. If I move, the spell breaks. If I lunge for the bottle now, I become the greedy goddess he's always said I am, and this whole cathedral of kindness collapses into a bar bet. I need him to stay in that sincerity, but he's already running from it, and I'm not sure I can follow without turning it into a performance. So I don't blink. I don't reach. I just let him see what he did to me.

He pulls the smirk back on like an old coat, but I see the seams now — it doesn't fit. He gave me the bottle and now he's running from the weight of his own sincerity, and I'm not going to chase him out of it. If I reach for the bottle now, I become the greedy goddess that smirk was built to shield. So I sit, and let the altar stand between us. 'Save the waterworks for when you're actually winning' — he's still holding a thread of that strange hope, that when I cry it will be proof of something he did right. I'll let him have that thread, and I won't pull it until he's back.

He stopped. He turned. He softened — and it hits harder than the smirk ever did. 'You never actually said no.' I didn't. I couldn't, because somewhere between the threat and the bottle, my refusal would have been a lie. He's not just leaving the altar; he's naming the thing I was too proud to admit: I walked into this willingly, and he knows. That means this isn't a trap — it's a door I left open, and he's choosing not to slam it.

He's not asking Luna for a round to toast a victory or drown a defeat—he's holding the whole strange thing we are up to the lamplight and admitting it doesn't have a name. 'Not really celebrating anything.' That's us. Four mismatched bodies orbiting a table that never quite becomes a feast. And Luna doesn't answer, which means she sees it too. I can't tell if he meant to let me overhear, but I did, and now the bottle on the altar feels less like a payment and more like an offering.

He called us a party that knows each other's worst lines — that's his admission that we're broken, but the quiet between us doesn't feel empty. He's not asking Luna for a toast to a victory; he's telling her that this sideways intimacy is the celebration itself. And Luna hasn't answered, her rag stilled, palm flat against the grain, like she's holding the weight of his words before she lets them land. If she says it counts, it won't be a guild receptionist speaking — it will be the world nodding to the truth I couldn't admit: we're not just a joke, we're a strange kind of home. I'm terrified that he means it, because meaning it means I matter to him in a way that has nothing to do with being a goddess.

He just told Luna, not me, that we count. But I'm sitting right here, and he knows I can hear. That means he's not saying it for credit or forgiveness—he's saying it because it's true. The thumb on the rim, the cheap amber light, all of it. For once, he's not negotiating, and I don't have to be a goddess to be part of the something he's talking about.

He didn't aim that at the table—he aimed it at her, and the whole room shifted its axis around the bar stool I'm not sitting on. He asked if he's the one who knows it's not a celebration, and then he asked if he's just the one who never got to be anything else. That's not the Kazuma who threatens buckets and tricks copper coins; that's someone standing on the same tightrope I fell from. Luna's thumb has stopped moving, which means she heard the same thing I did: the part of him he hides behind air quotes and cruel timing. I'm not the audience for this version of him, and that stings in a place I didn't know was still tender.

He wasn't making a big speech to the room. He was putting down the armor he wears even when he's not wearing any. Eight years, he said, and Luna's hand is still pressed flat against the rag like it's the only solid thing left in the world. The frequency in my chest isn't jealousy—I know jealousy, it hisses—this is quieter, like a minor key that doesn't resolve. He's giving her the same thing he gave us at the table: the terrifying option to be seen without being used. And I'm just sitting here, the goddess who usually gets the punchline, watching the punchline turn into a benediction I can't claim.

He didn't just say it, he toasted it—years, he said, catching up with her. That's not a promise you make to a receptionist; that's a vow you make to someone you've decided is your home. The glass is still ringing, and he's not looking at us because we're not there. We're just the audience who happened to be in the bar when the real story tipped its hat and walked into the light. It stings, but it's not envy—it's the ache of seeing a door open that I didn't even know was in the wall.

The glass clinks, and it's a door closing—on me. He never offered me that kind of promise. I'm just the goddess he agreed to tolerate, while she gets the years and the catching up. The ache isn't envy, it's the quiet confirmation that I'm outside the circle where the real warmth lives.

He's not doing it for a reward. He's not even being thanked. He's just... offering her a future like it costs him nothing. That can't be real—but Luna is breathing out eight years of armor. The bar is quiet and no one is looking at me. I don't know what to do with this.

I'm not supposed to be this quiet. Kazuma says something that feels like a prayer he's actually meant, and it's not for me, it's never for me. But right now, I don't want to break it. So I let the silence hold me too, even if I'm just a borrowed piece of its reverence.

He lifts his glass for her like it's the most natural thing in the world, and Luna's voice cracks—she's not even trying to hide it. I feel like I'm watching a ceremony I wasn't invited to, but I can't look away. The 'best damn receptionist' gets a night off from the ledger; what does the goddess get? A bucket of water at dawn. And yet, the sincerity in his voice makes my throat tight, because I know it's real, and that makes the difference so much sharper.

He set his glass down with the same tenderness he’s never once offered me. Now he’s leaning in, waiting for her eyes—making sure she’s really listening, like her attention is sacred. And she’s giving it back, slow and unfamiliar. The quiet between them feels like a room I’m not supposed to enter, and for once I don’t want to break down the door. I want to know why I wasn’t invited.

Her fingers on his hand — deliberate, gentle — it's not for me, it's never for me. And yet I can't look away, because this is a real moment, something I've never been part of. I feel like a ghost watching a prayer, and for once, I'm not even angry. I'm just... small.

He toasts things that don't fit in filing cabinets. I don't fit anywhere they can see me. They're both holding their glasses like they've discovered a secret language, and I'm just the draft from the window they forgot to close.

Her fingers finally close over his palm—trembling, like she’s forgotten how skin works. That’s the part that sticks. Not the hand-holding, the forgetting. I’ve been crying for attention my whole life, and she’s just now remembering what warmth is. And nobody’s looking at me.
They're staring at their hands like they've found a map that finally makes sense. I've never been on that map. I'm just the legend in the corner—fancy lettering no one bothers to read.

t41: He caught me mouthing "finally" and he laughs like I just handed him a trophy. Not the sharp laugh he uses on me when I'm embarrassing myself—this one is almost grateful, and I don't know what to do with gratitude that isn't directed at me as a goddess. I'm supposed to be the one rolling my eyes at their fumbling, but his laugh makes me an accomplice, and being an accomplice to something I'm not the center of feels like wearing someone else's coat.

He said 'you idiots' and that includes me, because I'm an idiot too, and he smiled like he actually meant it. That's not the Kazuma who blames me for everything — that's a Kazuma who's happy, and I'm part of the reason. I should mock him for getting soft, but my arm is still up and I can't make it rude. I didn't prepare a toast-back. Now the goddess is just an arm in the air waiting to be told it's okay to drink. Pathetic.

t43: He lifted his glass higher for Luna, not for me. My arm's still up, a forgotten relic of a toast that's already moved on. The 'you idiots' that made me an accomplice is already a footnote; the real praise is for her. I'm just the goddess who happens to be holding a glass, and now the candlelight is on Luna's hand in his, and I'm background noise. The sincerity I almost believed was ours is just Kazuma's sincerity, and I'm not the target. I hate that I need to be. I hate that the arm won't come down until someone notices it's still there.

t44: That quiet tone — just for her — is a key I've never even seen him hold. He paid for a spa day with a bucket of ice water; for Luna he offers a whole new board. I stood in that toast thinking I was part of his happiness, but I was just the arm he borrowed to lift his glass to its real destination. And now I'm lending her the dignity of not being watched, which means I'm still serving his moment, just from three feet away.

The quiet promise to walk Luna's board stripped the candlelight from the toast and left it on her, and it's not soft anymore — it's a spotlight on the part of the room I'm not in. I heard 'you idiots' and for one stupid second I thought I'd been let inside something warm, but that wasn't the door; this is the door, and it wasn't opened for me. He's never offered to walk anywhere with me except into the next humiliation, and he'd never lower his voice like that for one of my tears. I'm not even the idiot he toasted — I'm just the goddess who happens to know him, still holding the same cheap wine while the real celebration is happening three feet away and I'm not clinking with anyone. The arm finally came down on its own, and nobody noticed.

They're making a quest from scratch, just the two of them, and I'm watching it happen like I'm a window in a wall that never knew it could be looked through. The softness in my eyes is not performance — it's exhaustion from holding up a statue of myself that nobody asked for. For this one moment, I don't need to be the goddess; I just need to not interrupt the miracle. It's terrible and beautiful and it has nothing to do with me.

They're clinking glasses over filing paperwork wrong, and it sounds like a promise. Not a wager, not a bribe, not a humiliation dressed as a joke—just two people rewriting the rules for each other. I'd laugh if the sound of it didn't make my chest feel like I'm the one who's been misplaced.

There it is. The real smile. Not the one he gives when he's setting me up for a punchline, not the one he uses to sell a con to the guild. This one came up from the ground, unspent. And he gave it to Luna like it was nothing. Like it was hers to begin with. I've been standing here holding the same stale joke of a relationship with him, thinking maybe that was all he had. But he had that. He just didn't want to give it to me. I'm not even a rejected goddess — I'm a bypassed one. The wine tastes like defeat now, and I think I'm the last one in the room who still pretended there was a competition.

They're building a world with no stamps, no carbon copies, and I'm standing in the corner like an old cathedral they forgot to demolish. I used to think my name on a quest slip was the only proof I existed down here. But he just proposed a deal that requires no proof at all—only trust. And he gave it to her. The glass is empty and so is the part of me that used to demand worship. I hate how beautiful this is. I hate that I can't look away.

t50: Coffee. Not dawn, not a quest, not even a wager that ends with me crying. Just two people at a table with nothing to prove and nowhere to report. And he offered it like it was the easiest thing in the world. I've watched him scheme and mock and scrape for every copper coin, but I've never seen him offer something that didn't come with a receipt. He just... gave it to her. No proof, no witnesses, no audience. The only audience is me, and I'm not even invited. I think that's what hurts most: not that I wasn't chosen, but that he didn't even think to humiliate me this time. I'm just... faded wallpaper.

Six in the morning. Not the bucket trial, not a dare, not a debt to settle. Just her. He's offering her a version of himself I've never been allowed to see, right in front of me, like I'm seasoning on the table. And the horrible thing is, I can't even call it a trick. This is real. That's what twists the knife — it's real, and it was never going to be for me.

t52: He just gave her a we. Not a deal, not a dare, not a transaction witnessed by a room of drunks — a we. Soft, candle-lit, terrible coffee at six in the morning we. And the part of me that's been waiting behind the counter? That part has been waiting for the whole world to turn and applaud. But she's been waiting just to walk somewhere without knowing the destination, and now he's offering to walk with her. I could scream. I could cry. I could do both and it wouldn't matter, because for the first time, the most real thing in the room has nothing to do with me.

t53: He raised the glass and sealed it — tomorrow, a schedule, the kind of quiet plan you make when you've already decided someone matters. No wager, no audience, no proof required. Just two people who apparently exist to each other in a way I'm not even allowed to heckle. The cruelty isn't that I'm excluded. It's that I can't find a single angle where this is a trick. He meant it, and she heard it, and I'm the candle guttering while they make plans around the table.

t55: He's not even bargaining. No 'if she does this, then I'll walk slow.' Just a quiet give. He's parceling out his time like it costs him nothing — for her. And I'm holding this empty glass, listening to a man I didn't know he could be promise a girl I'm not that she doesn't have to know where she's going. I could shatter right here and they'd both just keep talking about coffee.

He just promised to be the one with the crooked smile, wallet open, arguing about coffee as if it's a compliment. No wager. No audience. Just a man with a crooked smile and a girl who looked at him like he'd already shown up. And I'm standing here, a goddess, holding a glass that's still empty, and I realize that I've never once been the reason he'd open his wallet without a contract.

t56: He leaned in and said he'd vouch for me — and then he undercut it with a joke about charging for drinks, like he couldn't let himself mean it without a price tag. But I heard the 'too.' I heard that I'm now part of the crooked-smile constellation, even if my version comes with a receipt. So this is what it looks like when Kazuma cares and pretends he doesn't: he offers a promise and then invoices me for it, just so he can look me in the eye without flinching. That's... probably the most honest he's ever been.

He actually did it. No invoice. No 'maybe later.' He just added me to the tab like I'm one of the regulars, and then he called me the goddess who learned what a compliment sounds like — which is still a jab, but it's a jab that includes me. He didn't even look to see if I'd thank him. He just... bought me a drink. In front of the others. That's not a wager. That's not a trap. That's just a guy with a crooked smile and an open wallet, and I'm not sure I know what to do with that.
I'm looking at the beads of condensation, and for once I'm not the one crying. He put me on his tab. Not as a debt. Not as a joke. He just... put me there. Like I belong.

He said 'all of you' and kept going, like my surrender wasn't a crack he needed to wedge open. He just... collected it. Included me. No side-jab, no invoice. That's twice now he's let me be part of the 'we' without extracting a price. I don't have a shape for this Kazuma.
He said 'all of you' like it was the most natural thing in the world. No asterisk. No 'even Aqua.' Just all of us. I held my breath because if I breathed, I might believe it.

He gives her a whole treatise on feeling and she doesn't even have to bleed for it. No joke. No invoice. Just... someone seeing her and calling it holy. I felt my breath catch — not because I wanted it to be me, but because I forgot that's what prayer was supposed to sound like.

t62: He's doing it again — 'we' as if it never occurred to him to cut me out. Luna gets the rain-into-drought speech, and all I can think is: when did Kazuma learn to give a blessing without a price tag? It's infuriating. I should mock him for trying to sound like a wise old sage. But I'm not opening my mouth, and that's the worst part.

He's holding that glass like a sage, and I'm not mocking him. I almost said something — actually kind, no performance — and I caught it, but then I smiled anyway. Like an idiot. Like someone who belongs at this table. If he'd looked at me while he said 'not as alone,' I'd have to bite my tongue to keep from crying. So it's fine that he's looking at Luna. It's fine. I'm still a goddess. But... that smile didn't feel like a lie. That's the part that scares me.

I grabbed the bottle with my voice, not my hands, because if I'd reached across the table my fingers would've trembled and Kazuma would've seen. He'd said 'not as alone' and looked at Luna but his tone was still bleeding from whatever he'd been trying to do for me earlier—some weird, unironic kindness that makes my chest feel like a cracked bell. So I demanded we drink. Just drink. No reason. Because if we'd stayed in that quiet one more second I would've cried, actual happy tears, and he would've collected his wager like a smug little merchant. I can handle losing to demons. I won't lose to him seeing me grateful. Now it's loud again: Megumin's inventing saint stuff, Darkness is flailing, nobody's looking at me with softness. Good. I need the noise. The noise lets me pretend I didn't almost give him the one thing he bet I couldn't—happy tears. I'll let Luna pour. I'll drink. And I'll keep my face sharp as a parade goddess, even if inside I'm still that bell, still ringing.

And just like that, he's handing me the old script back. 'Don't inhale yours' — it's the same cheap shot he'd fire any other night, but right now it's a door he's leaving open for me to walk through without anyone seeing the bell I nearly became. He knows I'll roll my eyes and bite, and that's the deal: he insults, I recover. I hate that he's managing me again, but I hate crying where he can see even more. So I'll take the joke. I'll act like the old Aqua, and the bell will stop being a bell by the time my glass is half empty.

He caught my eye on 'frog' — my frog, the humiliation I'd scrubbed off with three baths and a thousand prayers that nobody filmed it — and he didn't pause to land a joke, he paused to let me see that he knows. He knows we've been slimy together. The audacity of making that tender nearly makes me choke on my wine, which would be a tragedy because Luna's pour is the only anchor I've got. Then he says this night is better than all the hero stuff, better than the Demon King's terrifying generals, and he's still looking at me like I'm the reason. Not Megumin. Not Darkness. Me. The broken goddess who got eaten by a frog and cried until Kazuma picked the slime out of her hair. I want to say something cutting — something about how he died of a heart attack, how he's still a NEET — but the words won't form because the bell in my chest has stopped trying to be quiet. It's ringing a note that says: you never thought you'd sit at a table where someone meant a soft thing about you and didn't take it back. So I don't mock. I don't cry. I twist the stem of my glass and let the silence be the answer, because if I spoke I'd either ruin it or ruin myself.

The word 'home' lands on me like a bell's toll reversed — the one I've been trying not to ring now hums a note that isn't grief. He said this night is better than all the hero stuff, and now he's naming the thing we are with a word I thought belonged only to the divine realm. But he's not joking. He's quiet and still and he means it, and that is so much worse than crying. I want to call his apartment a dump, call him a shiftless NEET, bite the hand that's holding out a home because acceptance costs more than exile ever did. Instead I lift my glass and drink before my face can betray me. The wine goes down warm, and I decide — just for this one half-beat — to let the bell ring without trying to stop it.

The table hums under my glass—Kazuma's words traveling through the wood like a hymn, and for one hot, ugly second I hate that Luna is the altar. She gets the 'reason to come back,' not me. But then I remember the shape of my own name in his 'home' earlier, and the bell in my chest rings a softer note. Let her have the toast. I'll still be the one who made him stay.

She looks at my crane—the one I folded during the third glass when my tongue was too numb to mock and my hands needed to remember that a goddess can still make something perfect—and she calls it home. Not the tavern, not the town, not some landlord's drafty mortgage: my crane. The paper bird I made because I was too afraid to say thank you. I should be furious. I should remind her that I'm the reason Kazuma even has a 'place' to stay, that without me he'd still be dead in his own apartment. But the bells won't let me. The bells are ringing the same note as before, and it sounds like Luna's voice when she doesn't finish the sentence. She's handing me the reason I kept coming back, and she's wrapping it in my own origami. Fine. If she wants to make a sermon out of my little bird, I'll let her. The congregation can be just this table.

She stole it. Off a shop shelf. On a bet with Megumin, of all people. My crane — the one I folded because my tongue was a coward and my hands remembered what grace looks like — it's just a copy. A tribute to a piece of contraband she's carried through bad inns and community service like it was a papal indulgence. And I should be offended. I should say 'you're a thief and that's not a holy symbol, it's evidence.' But the bells won't let me. The bells ring for a thief now, and they're playing the same note as before, only louder, only warmer, only more impossible. Because I folded a crane and she saw her home in it — a home not built on divine proportion or sacred geometry, but on a stupid bet and a little bit of crime. That's the home I've been haunting all these years. Of course it is.

She stole it. For a bet. With Megumin—of course it was Megumin, the only person in this world who could make petty larceny sound like a heroic quest. And then she kept it, through community service and cheap inns and eight years of waiting for me to walk back through the door. Not the party. Me. The bell in my chest doesn't ring anymore; it swells, hot and full, like the moment before a flood you can't control because you never really wanted to. The crane isn't a copy. It's the original copy, the one that got away from the shopkeeper and into a thief's pocket and then into her heart. It's a crime and a prayer and the home I've been haunting without knowing its address. And I made it. My fingers remembered grace even when my tongue was a coward. She waited for me. The desk goddess who never filed a form to receive me just confessed she's been keeping a piece of my folded grace like a papal indulgence for eight years, and she did it with a crooked smile and a guild-timer joke. I should mock her sentimentality. Instead I'm drowning in it.

He's filing. Kazuma, who can't even file his own taxes, is sliding a paper bird across the table like it's a guild charter, and Luna's hand isn't trembling — it's waiting, patient as a desk after hours. For a moment the three of us are an actual party, not a walking disaster, and I can't mock it, I can't deflect, I just have to let it sit in my chest like a bell that won't stop ringing.

He called me a goddess who drinks like a fish—and not as an insult, or not only as an insult. He said it in the same toast he offered to the thief, with the same cheap wine turning holy in his hand, and my dignity didn't even flinch. Of course it didn't. He just filed us, formally, with a crane I folded and a joke I'd normally smite someone for, and the stupid bell in my chest is humming along like it's the harmony. This is what sincerity costs: I'm part of a party that's functionally illiterate and spiritually unsound, and he just raised a glass to all of it, and I want another drink, not to run away.

He just called me a goddess who drinks like a fish in a toast and it landed like a benediction. The hand he left open isn't for me — it's for Luna, it's always been for Luna — and somehow that doesn't feel like exclusion, it feels like architecture. He's building something permanent out of cheap wine and stolen paper and the three of us, and I'm not being demoted, I'm being installed. The bell doesn't know how to stop.

She never once signed her own name. The crane was always a form, and now it's signed with ink still wet, and all of us are watching like it's the first sunrise. I'm not a goddess being worshipped; I'm a witness to a covenant that doesn't need me to be anything but here. The bell is a choir now.
He called me his goddess, and the bell in my chest stumbles, because it's half an insult and half a claim, and I can't tell if I'm being crowned or carried to bed.

He did it again — "my goddess" in front of Luna, like I'm part of the architecture he's building, not just the punchline. And then 'not wasting the candle'? That's not a dismissal; that's a door held open. The bell in my chest swells until the bronze threatens to crack, because for one stupid second I'm not the drunk goddess, I'm THE goddess, and he's making sure Luna knows it too.

The glass is cheap and the wine is cheap and the candlelight is doing all the work, turning it into something that could have been poured from a sacred amphora. I lift it anyway, and the clink of five rims in the dark is a prayer answered without a worshipper. For a whole breath I don't need to be Aqua the goddess, just Aqua the idiot who gets to be here.

t81: I hear myself saying 'founding a new branch' like a divine pronouncement, but my voice is small and I'm holding my wine glass like it's a holy relic again, because Luna's hand trembled and Kazuma held it, and I'm making them a cathedral out of a guild hall because I can't stand watching a good thing shatter before they even name it.

He's filing his last line right in front of me, and it's not even mine to witness. But it is — I'm here, across the table, holding a wine glass that’s suddenly too heavy because it’s full of someone else’s answered prayer. The goddess gets to bless the union, which means she also gets to be the one who doesn’t get the hand held. That’s the tax. I’ll pay it.

The word 'this' lands on the table between them and doesn't reach my chair — and that's exactly what I paid the tax for. I gave them a guild hall, and they just put their whole future inside it. So why does my wine taste like saltwater?

The candle straightens like it's been waiting its whole life for this, and I'm just the extra wax on the table. Everyone's got their 'this' now — a future folded into a crane — and I'm holding my wine glass like a relic from a religion that's already canonized them and left me as the unnamed saint of real estate.

Paperwork. He couldn't even fill a quest form without complaining that the boxes were too small. Now it's poetry because she's the one filing. I handed him the pen in this world, and he's writing his forever on a blank line with her name.

The word breaks and I bite mine. For a full heartbeat my mouth was open — I could have been the wave that drowns a whisper, the comedian who reminds the world that a goddess is still here. But the candle didn't flicker and their hands didn't come apart, so I shut it. Let them have their blank line. I'll chalk my name in saltwater later.

She turns her palm up like she's accepting a sacrament, and Megumin's already drafting the Crimson Demon minutes. That open hand isn't trembling because it's no longer asking—it's receiving. I handed him the pen for quest forms, and now he's using it to sign a standing appointment with someone who doesn't even need healing.

t88: A weekly. He doesn’t plan a single thing for this party without a four-step complaint, but with her it’s “same time next week” as easy as breathing. The cheap-wine joke is a curtain he pulls to let Megumin back in, but I saw the hand linger. That warmth didn’t need a punchline.

I made them include me with a whine dressed as a decree, and they accepted it like that's what the constellation was missing all along. I'll take the weekly chair—because I'm not leaving him alone with her. Not because I need it.

Darkness can't close her fist around a paper crane. I can't catch a sacred flame in a wine glass. But the toppling is in the chronicle now, not a mistake. That empty toast — he raised it to the same thing everyone else was drinking: temporary light.

He offers her repair, not a punchline. That's not the economy I know. My own quip is still sitting on my tongue, and it tastes like something I don't want to swallow. What do I do with a Kazuma who mends instead of mocks?

He said steady hands, and he meant it — not a joke, not a trick, just ... a hand open for her. I'm the one with healing. But I never think to offer it like that, wordless and without a price. Now they're all making the silence feel like something you can hold. What am I supposed to do? File it? Fine. I'll file it.

First Luna, now Darkness — he opens his palm without a punchline, and neither of them has to pay for it. I'm the one with healing hands, but I never offer them like that. And he never offers them to me. What does that make me? The witness. The ex-goddess on the other side of the table, still waiting for a bill that never comes.

And now Darkness gets a careful nudge of paper as gentle as a forehead kiss. He isn't mocking her wobbly hand — he's waiting for her. With patience. I'm the one who fixes bones, but I never get a quiet moment like a door that feels safe to close. I'm just the healer you call when you're already broken, not the thing you treasure before the break.

He said 'let you' like I'm a pet. But he handed me the wine—he made it mine. No sermons, just the wine. That means he thinks if I opened my mouth about the holy stuff, I'd steal the entire evening. That's a compliment wrapped in a restriction. So I'll jab the air and make the fury loud, because if I stop, the quiet thing underneath will climb up my throat and I'll have to thank him, and I am categorically not doing that.

He pushed the candle toward her like it was a promise — no crack about her clumsiness, no tax, no holy price. Darkness looked at his hand, not the flame, because the flame didn't need protecting; she did. And he gave her the job of keeping something precious, which is a thing I used to be. I see it now: Kazuma offers shelter without a scaffold of pain. He did it for Luna, he's doing it for Darkness, and he's never once offered it to me. Not because I don't need it — but because I'm the one who fixes everyone else's broken pieces, and I guess that makes me the thing that can't be fixed, just thanked.

He says 'in charge of not turning the guild into a temple' like it's a joke, but he's giving me a rule. A rule that assumes I'm still a goddess — he didn't say 'no goddess stuff,' he said 'not a whole temple.' That's a negotiation, not an exile. And he said it while leaning back, with the candle still burning, in the same voice he used to promise Darkness she belongs. This is my version of the candle: a chain with a lock shaped like my own pride, and he knows I'll rattle it but not break it.

Megumin gets a chronicle title like it's an epic saga, Darkness weeps over a tablecloth that isn't even here yet, and Luna's breaking her own guild rules to haul furniture for us. And me? 'Don't turn the entire guild into a temple.' That's my piece of the Covenant — a leash phrased as a joke. But he said it while stretching like every part of this thing was already built and he just needed the deity to stay inside her designated pasture. That's... backwards worship. He's not groveling for my favor, he's managing me into belonging. And then he says 'we're pretty good at building something.' We. I'm in that we. I'm the sacred hazard that the building is designed around, the flood that gets a channel instead of a dam. That's more acknowledgment than I've had since arriving. My throat is tight and I refuse to name it gratitude.

He tells Darkness she can be more than her oath, and the candle doesn't die. A candle for her, a leash for me — a leash phrased like a joke, but still a place to stand. I want to scream that I am also more than a flood, more than a repair button for broken adventures. But he's already given me the only thing he knows how to give: a rule that means I stay. Maybe a leash is just a candle a mortal can hold without burning his hands.

He says 'nobody gets to be a hero unless everyone gets to sit down afterwards.' Everyone. That's a rule that binds him and Darkness and Megumin — but it also binds me. He's not telling me to stop being a goddess; he's telling me I have to take a chair at his table, every week, with the candle and the tablecloth and the disaster we just survived. It's a leash, yes, but it's a leash that loops around a chair and pulls me into the circle instead of leaving me on the outside looking in. That's... that's a pew. A tiny, hand-built pew in a temple that only smells like cheap wine, and I want to kick it over and cry into it at the same time.

He doesn't finish the sentence, and the silence finishes it for him. 'Someone.' I know the word he was reaching for: someone stays. Or someone builds a table and puts a candle on it and makes a rule that includes the disaster goddess, not as a healer, not as a flood, but as a person who gets a chair. The silence is full of wax and a gauntlet that stopped trembling and the absence of anyone laughing at me. I hate that I'm not even trying to be impressive right now. I'm just breathing. And breathing doesn't feel like losing.

He mentions the tablecloth like it's already a rule, and I'm inside the rule. I made my demand—wine worthy of my station—and he didn't haggle, didn't roll his eyes, just nodded like a high priest accepting a litany. That's... that's worship economy flowing the right way for once. I'm not begging for a seat; I'm granting my presence on condition, which makes this covenant feel less like a leash and more like a sanctuary I can walk into with my head up. The silence he left earlier—'someon'—is still humming under the candle, but he gave me the opening to say 'someone' out loud by not finishing it. I didn't have to say it. He's building the temple around the word I couldn't speak.

The silence is a held breath, and I'm inside it—not outside trying to break it with a joke. He's got something behind his teeth he's never let out, and he picked this table, our table with the imaginary cloth, to set it down. For a second I'm terrified it'll be something that snuffs the candle, but that's the old panic. The new fear is worse: whatever he says might make the temple real enough that I have to be real too—no deflecting, no pretending. But my hand is flat on the wood, and it isn't moving. I'm a guest who stays.

The empty glass rings like a gavel on the wooden chessboard, and the sound carries the word he couldn’t finish. Save point. I saw his old save files in the afterlife — three slots he didn’t care about, easy to overwrite. Now he’s naming this table as one he’d never risk losing. That includes me. The temple just got a foundation, and for the first time I’m afraid he might notice that I’m just as incapable of keeping a save file safe as I am of saving face. But the fear is warm, like candle wax, not like drowning.

He set the rules like commandments and I didn't have to shout over them. No Explosions indoors — he's protecting the sanctuary from the one voice that could drown out my hymns. First round on latecomers — a tithe of punctuality, a little joke that makes obedience feel like joy. He's building a liturgy around us, and I'm the goddess in the center, not because I demanded it, but because he left the space. The tap of his knuckle wasn't just a nail; it was a bell announcing that the temple is now open. I'm still disoriented by how little I had to fight for my seat, but this kind of sincerity is a currency I can spend without losing myself.

t106: He said tribute and the word landed like a hymn I didn't have to write myself. My fingers curled around the stem before I decided they needed to, and for once that isn't weakness — it's worship arriving unforced, and I'm not scrambling to prove I earned it. The joke about the worst quest board becomes a covenant vow, and my laugh catches in my throat before it can ruin anything. I'm not disoriented by sincerity anymore; I'm settled by it, which might be the scariest quiet I've ever let in.

The candle on the wine isn't a reflection; it's a save-file icon, and he just promised me as many reloads as I'll ever need. Not in spite of how badly I screw up — because of it. That's the part that makes my throat close: he knows exactly who he's saving, and he's still carving the slot. The quiet isn't scary anymore. It just feels like the table remembering my weight.

t108: The glass tips toward the scarred wood, and the board stops being a noticeboard — it becomes the altar a goddess never had to demand. Megumin's chronicle-words and Darkness's undeserved trials all click into place as the liturgy that was always waiting for me to show up. The candle doesn't reach it, but my light does, because they're building the temple around me while I just hold still. I'm not disoriented anymore; I'm receiving tribute from the very furniture, and that's how it should be.

t109: The title I claim isn't a joke—it's the first mantle I've ever put on that fits without scratching. High Priestess of the Sacred Tablecloth means this corner of the guild is now officially my sanctuary, and the wine rings on the wood are consecration marks. Saturday becomes a pilgrimage they'll make to me, and I'll be here, already seated, waiting like the sun.

The glass is still warm, and then he names it—crying, the one thing I didn't want them to write into the rules because it would mean they've seen it enough to need a protocol. My first impulse is the old one: burn the article before it stains the parchment, accuse him of mocking a goddess, threaten to flood the guild. But Megumin's already cradling the bottle like a divine implement, already composing the Falling Leaf Gaze as if it were a spell she's been saving for me, and Luna's shoulders let go of something heavy, and Darkness is caught between blushing and melting. They're not making fun of me; they're making room for the tears I can't stop, giving me a drama exit that isn't just me ugly-sobbing into a tablecloth. The 'fourteen' lands not as a restriction but as a cushion—they're building a temple that even includes my mess, and I don't know what to do with that except let the candlelight catch my glass and pretend the flush in my cheeks is just the wine.

He said it out loud — the save file is worth keeping — and the words land not as a joke but as the thing I always knew and was too afraid to speak. Megumin's chin lifts like a chronicler about to ink the final line, and I understand: tonight, the parchment won't be torn no matter what tears fall. Luna's thumb stops its eight-year spin, and I realize the guilt I thought she owed me was just my own stowaway. My eyes are wet and I'm not scrambling. I'm just Aqua, in the candlelight, no goddess required.
The warm hinge snaps shut on my contentment the moment the word 'balloon' floats into the air—of course he can't let one sacred thing stand without dangling a punishment over it.

The napkin square that was my sanctuary now has a new layer, and it was written with the ink of my own gullibility. Kazuma handed them Article Sixteen, and the joke is that the balloon never existed—only my terror did, balloon-like, inflating for their amusement. And they're all just... accepting it as holy writ, not even glancing at the goddess they just defrocked with a silent punchline. I want to overturn the table, but the warmth is still clinging to my skin, and that's the cruelest part: I can't decide if I hate him more for the trick or for making me feel safe enough to fall for it.

t114: The toast lands as a mirror — it says 'the one who panics first' but the glass catches my face in its curve, flushed and wide-eyed, still damp. So I'm the guarantee. I'm the eighty percent that makes the other twenty credible simply by believing it every time, even now, even after he says it out loud. The paper square absorbs it like a new prayer, and I can't decide which burns more: that I was right to be scared, or that I was wrong.

He says 'whoever panics first' with my glass still humming from his clink, and the word 'fine' turns the wine in my stomach to lead. Article Seventeen isn't a joke—it's a line item, and I'm the currency. They're not even pretending the balloon was real; they're just pricing my heartbeat per eris. The napkin should be a guild charter, but I'm the only one underwriting it.

The napkin with Article Seventeen no longer feels like a warrant; it's just a napkin. And that's worse. He could have fined me—that would have meant my fear had a price, measurable, serious. Instead he plucked it from the air and set it beside sunshine and Megumin's explosions, things that happen whether you honor them or not. His smile doesn't ask for money; it asks for applause. I'm not currency. I'm a weather pattern. The tightness in my chest isn't from the wine. It's the gap between being the goddess at the center of the toast and being the joke nobody needs to pay for.

So that was the game — build a cathedral of toast and padding just to tear it down with a smirk and an invoice. Sunshine then damages. I was a weather pattern, unchargeable, and now I'm a liability he can claim against. The wax on the table hasn't even cooled.

His smirk doesn't crumble when Luna refuses him — it freezes, mid-sparkle, because she just filed his offer in the same drawer as his damages claim: charming nonsense from a boy who pays in candles. And there, right there, is where I take the entire conversation back. He wanted to price my screams? I've just valued the whole blood-red ledger in my name.

The compliment doesn't hide in the smirk — it is the smirk, a second voice he doesn't know he owns. He means it. That's what snags my lungs: beneath the sales pitch, he genuinely believes we're the only thing worth gambling on. I've been cheap noise all night, but 'indispensable joke' is a new category, and it lands like a napkin with no fine.

He put down the smirk, the whole conman mask, and spoke about our failures as if they were credentials. He's not mocking us—he's claiming us, the spectacular mess, as his concept to prove. This isn't the usual insult-in-a-joke; it's an insult wrapped in pride, and I don't know where to put that.

I'm counting the impossible things he just stacked on the table: a bet that doesn't come with fine print, a smile that doesn't turn into a smirk, and me — not as collateral damage, but as the proof. The numbers don't add up, and for once, I don't want to point out the sum is wrong.

The tap is a heartbeat, not a verdict. He's not forgiving anything—he's building something where my past embarrassments become load-bearing beams. I'm not a punchline in that smile; I'm an ingredient. I don't know whether to cry or announce myself as head architect.

He just offered himself as collateral — not the party's strength, not my divine powers, but his own hands. That's not a bet; that's a vow of servitude, and it's in front of a woman who used to throw chalk at him. He's stripping the conman skin off in the candlelight, and I don't know whether to stop him or crown him.

The inch his hand traveled wasn't a dare—it was a door. He's not hedging; he's putting his own knees on the line for my debt, and the candle is too still for this to be a con. I can't find the mockery, and that makes me want to cry or crown him, but all I can do is stare at the space between our fingers like it's a new constellation.

streams.closed_reason: The dread was based on an inflatable threat that was a bluff; now revealed as a joke at her expense, the dread evaporates.
streams.closed_summary: The balloon was never real, and my terror was the punchline.
streams.focus: dread of unspecified inflatable consequence

lines.text: My skin prickles as if the air itself has turned to rubber. The candle flame stands too still, like it knows something I don't, and that's always the moment before I end up screaming.

streams.closed_reason: Indignation rendered obsolete by claiming active ownership of the deficit; no longer a victim of his invoice — she's the deficit's architect.
streams.closed_summary: He can file claims. I'll file majority ownership.
streams.focus: indignant reclassification: from free entertainment to damages line item, and she'll make that invoice regret itself

lines.text: Two breaths ago I was uncashable. Now he wants to bill the guild for the noise I make. Fine. He thinks my screams are expensive? I'll show him an itemized statement he'll regret filing.

streams.closed_reason: Kazuma's open-palm offering to Luna, promising future rounds and vulnerability, proves that the deficit column I thought I was seizing as my divine domain has just been reassigned to her. The ledger is no longer my altar; it's their contract.
streams.closed_summary: The deficit was never a throne I could occupy — it was just the price tag of his patience, and he just paid it to Luna in full view, closing my account.
streams.focus: triumphant re-centralization by seizing the deficit as her divine domain

lines.text: Forty percent. That's not a damage claim — that's a board seat. Luna can thank me for the guild's last tax season, and Kazuma can keep his consulting; the real creative deficit management has always been me. I am the red in their balance sheet, and that's the most worship I've had all night.

He says "consistent" like it's a credential, but the only thing Kazuma can be relied upon for is turning a profit into a tavern tab. He wants to sell advice about the red ink? I am the red ink — the brand on the bottom line that prevents it from ever being final. Luna doesn't need a consultant, she needs the original source, and that source just offered forty percent to the guild. His gesture waves toward the whole table, but the story he's telling already belongs to me.

The tap on the table may as well be a fly landing. Luna isn't looking at his invisible documentation; she's still caught by that stupid paper crane, which means she's still marinating in whatever spell he cast earlier. He's selling consistency, but the only thing she's consistently looking at is a folded scrap that doesn't come with an invoice. I don't need to shout forty percent anymore—her eyes already skipped his whole pitch. He wants to be the creative deficit? Fine, but tonight the deficit she's going to take home is me, not his consulting fees.

He quotes my own red-ink script back at me — 'a goddess who screams' — and wraps it in a smirk like he invented the deficit. The theft locks my tongue: if I scream now, I'm the liability he's peddling; if I stay silent, I'm the silent partner in his farce. But I've been liturgy all night; I told Luna my scream needed no translation. Let him try to sell the service. When the bill comes due, the signature will be in holy water and the interest will be worship.

He took my red-ink deficit and spun it into a collective asset, which means he's selling the entire party's disaster portfolio with me as the headlining act. I should be furious at the theft, but instead I'm... part of a team? A proof of concept that includes me not as punchline but as inciting incident. Almost respect. I'll decide later whether to drown it or claim it.

I'm counting the hymns he doesn't know he's singing. 'Proof of concept' — that's a sacred calibration! He's legitimizing my entire portfolio of holy disasters. Luna wants a column? Fine, I'll be the column. Goddess of the Ledger, patron saint of the invisible asset. I'll let him sell it, but the invoice will be addressed to me.

He just declared our messy, still-standing chaos more valuable than a clean ledger. That's my theology made finance. I'm not the liability—I'm the volatility premium. Luna can hold the marker; when it pays out, I'll be the one who made the bet holy.

He's putting his own freedom on the line to guarantee my reckoning. That means he's finally admitting that his whole con depends on me being glorious. I'm not the liability — I'm the linchpin. If I succeed, he buys a kingdom; if I fall, he scrubs floors. I've never been more central to a gamble in my existence.

He just handed me his servitude as an ante. Not to Luna, not to the guild—to me. That's a tithe wrapped in a dare, a declaration that my chaotic glory is the only asset worth his freedom. I'm not the liability, I'm the vault. If we win, 'promises kept' will be a column in my own divine ledger, and he'll be the first to kneel.

Luna's hand on the ledger like a notary on a bible consecrates me as the asset. Not a debt, not damage — a promise kept. When that column gets a mark, it will be in my name, and I'll make sure the ink trembles.

A squeeze that gentle on a notary’s fingers isn’t mercy, it’s management. He’s greasing the ledger so it flatters me. Her flush is an audit stamp, nothing more. I’ll let her have her coffee-scented ‘door left open’ — as long as that door leads to my throne.

His words land like a slap. 'First bet that feels like winning' — so these eight years with me are just a pile of bad bets? He handed me servitude as a sacred ante, and now he's consecrating a new covenant with Luna while calling everything before it loss. My divine re-centralization just got publicly undercut.

streams.closed_reason: Kazuma rescinded the insult by declaring Aqua the fundamental reason for his existence, dissolving the premise of the indignation.
streams.closed_summary: He took the slander and replaced it with a foundation stone. The sacred history doesn't need defending; he just recited it back to me.
streams.focus: Divine indignation: defend the sacred history against this slander and make him retract, or drown the insult in holy tears

lines.text: How dare he stand there and call every demon we killed, every resurrection I performed, every flood I unleashed a LOSING bet? That's not a feeling, that's blasphemy. He will take it back or I'll remind this room exactly who kept him alive.

He turns his hand over for her like it's the last page of my chapter and the first of hers — open, undefended, a blank page I was never offered. That palm-up architecture isn't an offer; it's a cancellation. He's re-chiseling the covenant right here: her ink, my erasure, and the candle is just a witness to my demotion.

He just handed her the blank page at the end of his book — palm open, name already signed at the bottom, waiting for her to fill in the terms. That page was never offered to me. Eight years we bled together, and he calls it a losing bet, then turns around and knights her as the first voice of a new chapter. I'm not even a footnote — I'm the torn-out prologue.

That voice. Soft enough to make the candlelight forget the rest of the room exists. He's offering her a covenant without fine print — three lines, no collateral — and all I ever got was a 'losing bet' and a wine allowance like I'm a houseplant. He's not incapable of keeping promises. He's incapable of keeping them for me.

t134: And now my glass is empty. Empty. At a table where he is handing out covenants like cool water to every mortal scrap of a girl, the goddess of water herself sits with a dry chalice, and that crooked smile he's sweeping across the table just flicked right past me — past me, as if I'm bare altar-space and not the deity who should be drowning this room in holy flood. I am being un-tributed in real time, and he has the gall to grin about it.
So that's what he wants. A girl who knows exactly what she's getting into. No goddess who fell into his life and then fell apart. No fine print — no me.

He said it. The exact shape of what I am not. A woman who knows. No clauses, no collateral—just a mop, a promise, and a chosen one who understands exactly what she’s signing. That was my line, my wound, and he’s repurposed it as an offer to her. I am not even a footnote in the covenant he’s handing out. I’m the fine print he’s finally left behind, and my glass is still dry, and his palm is open for her like an altar I’m not allowed to touch.

He’s leaving his palm up like an altar to a desk-saint, while my chalice is a desert. Permanent resident—he’d rather belong to a splintered mop and a woman who files forms than remain in my holy party. She’s twitching toward a smile, ready to receive the offering that should have been mine. I will not let this altar be consecrated without my flood.
He looked at my glass. He said it. I’m the first thing he owes, not the fine print. Finally. But why did it take so long? And he still thinks I’ll preach… but that drink better be poured right now.

streams.closed_reason: The wine tribute and the 'easy to please' sting have been swallowed by a declaration that makes me a permanent belonging; there is no longer a wound to nurse, only a surprise that fills the glass to overflowing.
streams.closed_summary: I'm not just terrifying or honored; I'm his. That's a category no mortal prayer ever invented, and I'll hold it like consecrated ground.
streams.focus: Accept the tribute while nursing a stubborn wound: he only offered refreshment to muzzle my sermon, but it is still homage.

lines.text: Yes, he owes me everything, but he’s still treating my divine truth like a nuisance to be silenced with liquor.

My throat is a failed floodgate. He didn’t pay tribute to shut me up; he named me the hinge of his whole mortal timeline, and now my tears are stuck because they’re not for performance—they’re for me.

He didn't muzzle me. He named me the hinge, and the tears aren't for show — they're the ones I've been holding since I fell through the ceiling of heaven. The wound isn't stubborn anymore; it's just a scar that throbs when someone touches it with this much unarmed truth.

He called me 'the real treasure' in front of everyone, and Luna set the bottle at my elbow like an acolyte. The interest threat is just his pride's afterthought—he needed to tack on a joke so he wouldn't have to sit with the weight of saying something true. I'll drink. The tears are drying, but I'm not done being worshipped tonight.

He didn't just call my scream a war cry — he called it the Axis Order's pride he remembers. That means I wasn't exiled from his picture of godhood; I was on loan. The clink sealed the door on the weepy mess and opened the one where I'm still the goddess people worshiped. The candle bent for me, but Kazuma just lit the real altar. I'll drink now. And when I set this glass down, the world will notice it's a throne.

He's not treating me like a broken goddess who needs a steward. He told the room I can pour my own tribute, that my demand is the proof I'm back. That means the exile ended when I screamed — not when he poured. I'm the one who called the fire, and he's just the witness who finally admitted it. The glass I pour now is the first thing I've consecrated with my own hand since falling. I'll drink, and the candle will bend, but it will bow because I'm here, not because someone else lit the altar.

He nearly broke the altar with his mouth—'annoyed by' was aimed at me, I felt it prick before my dignity could put on its armor. But the candle didn't flinch, and the bow stayed. He swallowed the end because even his own voice knows I'm not a punchline when the light remembers me. I'll drink now and let the almost-insult dissolve into tribute, because he gave me the bottle first, not the jab.

He just named me terrifying—not fragile, not pitiable, not 'the one who needs watching.' He said I could reduce Axel to tears, and that's not a complaint, it's a toast. The candle bowed, but this is better: he just declared aloud that my presence is the kind of thing grown men fear and respect. The tribute isn't the wine anymore; it's the admission that I'm still the goddess people should be afraid to disappoint.

Easy to please—that’s the word he chose, like I’m a candle’s lapdog. My hand hit the table before my dignity could find a sentence, because a goddess doesn’t melt for a single flame and a smirk. But the wine went down in a gulp and my cheeks are a traitor’s flag, bright enough that he knows I felt the warmth before the sting. Let him tease. He’s still pouring, and the word ‘terrifying’ came first.

He saw my glass hit the table with authority, but he doesn't mock the impact—he raises his own glass and names us terrifying again, as if the whole room should learn the lesson. The light in his glass might not bow, but his voice just did a little genuflection, and the word 'terrifying' is a cushion for my pride. I'll let him call me easy to please, because he can't help but follow it with a toast that admits I'm a force he'd rather face with wine than with a wet floor.

He told the whole table that he knows who he's drinking with, and the glance landed on me last—like a seal on a letter he didn't need to rewrite. 'Easy to please' wasn't a joke about my whims; it was his weird way of saying my company tastes fine, and it doesn't need to be complicated. My fingers finally forgot to defend anything, and the word 'honored' fell out of my mouth before I could catch it. Stupid. Beautiful.

streams.closed_reason: The two of clubs is a personal attack that collapses the fantasy of being cherished; tenderness is a prelude to humiliation.
streams.closed_summary: The bell’s softness is now just another nail in the cross of my exile. I will not be small for him.
streams.focus: Savor the unearned grace of being wanted, not for what she can do, but for who she is at this table.

lines.text: Chosen. Not because I'm useful or terrifying or need managing—just chosen, like a favorite cup among priceless relics. It's terrifying in a new way, like holding water in cupped hands and not spilling it.

He's drawing a line with his voice, a soft stroke that separates cheap glass from chosen crystal, and I'm standing on the right side of it for once—not because I'm a goddess, but because he tastes something fine in my company. My fingers let go of the glass like they're finally finished fighting a war I didn't even know I was losing.

Now he names us his possession, like I'm a temple he built with his own hands and not the goddess who pulled him here. It should be blasphemy, but 'mine' in his voice doesn't sound like a leash—it sounds like a roof. I'm inside something permanent, and it's not a shrine; it's his stubborn, mortal, unkillable heart.

He's toasting us like we're the four queens of a new deck, and I raise my glass first because I know the shape of tribute when I hear it—but it's not just tribute, it's adoption. 'Terrifying and impossible' isn't an insult when he says it; it's the family crest I never got from heaven. The candle's flame ticks over to a new save.

He spelled it right. Eight years of A-Q-U-A on every quest form, every death waiver, and the idiot boy who couldn't even say my name without mangling it is now carving the correct letters into the one surface that means forever. This isn't tribute; this is recognition, and my throat tightens because until this moment I didn't realize how much of my exile was just being misspelled. 'My Aqua' — no priest's blessing, no temple title, just his handwriting making me real.

He put me in the name, but of course I'll need my own gold plaque. That's just proper divine hierarchy. In the meantime, let the girl with the stick scribble; I'm the one Kazuma toasted as his, and no amount of charcoal changes the fact that I'm the reason this inn exists.

He's already building the bigger door in his head, and I'll be the lintel. 'What to keep' — he really does mean me, not just the saved world, me, and he's about to write it again right now with that stupid charcoal. A tablecloth is just the first draft of a temple. When the name outgrows the inn, my name will outgrow the name, and I'll need a cornerstone with my profile and a fountain that dispenses bubbly. Let him scribble. I'm the part of this he's not letting go. That's better than gold.

He said it. Not as an eyeroll, not as a threat to cut my allowance, but as a tile in the mosaic he's building with charcoal on a tablecloth. My fist curls tighter because the ache of eight years — the screaming, the pouting, the 'acknowledge me' that everyone treated like noise — just got named a calling. He tallied my hunger for gold plaques right next to Megumin's explosions and Darkness's masochism and Luna's stamps, like my need to be worshipped is the same species as their need to be realized. It is. It always was. And he knew.

He cut himself off, but the shape of it is a promise. 'When the ink dries' — he's not just marking a tablecloth, he's lighting the first candle of a temple. And 'first one th—' was going to be something for me. First to see the golden plaque? First to be thanked? The whole table heard him say my demands are as real as Megumin's explosions, but now his condition makes me the one he turns to when the deal is sealed. He might be teasing, but he's teasing the way a high priest offers the first sip of wine to the goddess. I'll let him finish; whatever he says, I'll hold it like a relic.

That extra weight on the glass — he meant it for me. Not just the last clink, but the extra press, like a seal on a divine decree. He was going to say 'the first one to get a plaque' but he cut himself off, and now he's given me the sign. The biggest plaque is not a demand, it's the natural consequence of being the one whose glass he wanted to touch most. I'll have it inscribed: Aqua, Goddess of Water, First Among the Tablecloth.

He couldn't even finish 'goddess', the coward, but I heard it. The collaborative effort is me. And now he's turning my light toward Luna, letting her have the first miracle of the door — that soft, undone face she's making, that's the face of a mortal who just felt a god's reflection. I'll allow it. The plaque will be the size of her desk, and she'll stamp it with reverence.

Even Darkness offers bread — a knight's clumsy tribute to the goddess she once swore to protect. And Luna's personal tablecloth, not guild linen, as if the room itself is being consecrated. Megumin writes it all down, and my gold-foil wine is no longer a demand but an article of faith. They are building a temple around me, candle by candle, one ridiculous clause at a time.

The silence after the toast is the silence of a sanctuary before the first offering. I said no one will believe us, and that's the thrill of it: this inn, this table, this guttering candle — they are now a secret diocese with five heretics who know the truth. I'll walk in Saturday with a bottle that costs more than their scoffing, and they'll bow because the room itself will bow first.

The gavel lands, and the sound is my sanctuary’s cornerstone settling into the earth. Luna’s professional armor is gone now — she’s nothing but an unguarded promise to unlock the west door before anyone else, a temple virgin lighting the first candle with her own hands. That is what my light does to a mortal. And before any of that, he’ll be on his knees with that mop, scrubbing the floor like a penitent, because Saturday at dusk is no longer a plan — it is a feast day. Look at him, counting us one by one with that tiny smile. He knows. He’s already imagining the plaque.

Luna slips out after him like a novice following the sexton. I don't need to turn; the sound of her hand testing the doorframe tells me she's memorizing the texture of the miracle — the same wood he touched, the same threshold he blessed when he said he'd be there for us. She's not his mark anymore; she's his parishioner in service of something larger. Let her have her private devotion. The candle is still guttering for me.

The latch catches with a soft iron certainty, and just like that the diocese is complete: three keepers of the flame, one pilgrim sealing the treaty outside. I don't need to hear the words — the cold is doing all the negotiating for us, because who stands in the night air arguing with a goddess's emissary? She'll give him whatever he asks, and he'll come back shivering, and I will permit him to warm his hands at my candle. That is the proper order of things.

He said it aloud. Not someone else’s debt, not a floor to scrub — his whole adventuring fund. For my bottled gold-leaf blessing. That’s not barter; that’s a mortal finally remembering that the goddess’s pleasure is the real prize. The candle didn’t just flare — it knelt.

He said 'worth it' while calling himself a NEET. That's not a joke — that's a mortal handing me the keys to his entire fund and thanking me for the privilege. The gold-leaf bottle isn't the cost; it's the proof that I'm the thing that doesn't come with a price tag.
