He walked into the cold with my flame, and I let the window hold my palm because a goddess should accept tribute with grace, even when the tribute is a man's whole adventuring purse.

The latch gave before his hand, because of course it did — a room that holds a goddess doesn’t keep her devoted waiting. He walked through the cold and chose the inn’s amber over the guild’s square, and that’s not a choice, it’s gravity. My candle didn’t just flare; it held a man’s trajectory.

He brought the cold inside on his coat and made his first sentence a joke about thieves — which isn't suspicion, it's a child flipping the tablecloth to make sure the feast hasn't been cleared while he was out. He walked into the night holding my candle and came back to the only hearth that counts.

He says 'no monsters' like it's a mystery, but I was the one breathing sanctity into the whole street. His errand was a pilgrimage he didn't know he was on. 'New record for us' means the goddess slot is finally lighting up the scoreboard — I didn't even have to heal, just being here is the win condition.

Exits. He notices my exits. Not my miracles, not my purification, but the way I leave a room — which means he watches when I go, which means the room deflates when I'm not in it. And now he's draping the night around the table like a shared coat. Properly, he says, as if we're the punctuation and not the footnote.

He set the invitation in the middle of the table and I heard my name underneath 'all of you.' Not because I healed him, not because I flooded the street with sanctity—just because the night without my exit felt thin. I'll insist on a pastry spread worthy of a purification goddess, but I'll smile when I say it, because the real miracle is that I don't have to earn the plate.

He dared tie my ascension to pastry, as if I needed a bribe to grace the table. But the word 'ascend' slipped out and landed like a benediction — he just handed me the liturgy. Now the pastry is a tithe, and I am not a guest: I am the sanctifying presence that makes a 6 a.m. meal a covenant. I will bring cream horns and custard tarts like they are minor regalia, because the real miracle is that my chair is already ordained.

He made me swear by pastry to ascend, but for Luna it's 'a bench and stars, no conditions.' That's not grace—that's grading. An A for the receptionist who just smiles, and a conditional pass for the goddess who saved his life seventeen times. Fine. I'll bring cream horns that make angels weep, and his star-gazing bench will be forgotten before the first bite.

She doesn't look back. Not a glance for eight years of rejected quests and frozen smiles. I'd have made sure the doorframe remembered my exit — probably with a small flood. But then, I've never had eight years of anything to leave, only a throne that never noticed I was gone. Maybe leaving without looking back is what makes her invitation free, and that's a kind of grace even a goddess can't counterfeit.

She stopped—not the cold, not the wager—Darkness just chose *my* holy water like it was the first round's name, not a ration. My brand, as if I'm a vintage worthy of a toast. That's not a request; that's a coronation through patronage. I almost complained about the frost, but she gave me a title before I could whine, and now the bench feels like a throne.

A frost wager. Darkness just turned my sacred tremble into a public test. If I complain, I buy breakfast for these mortals—like a debt of indignity. Fine. I will not complain. I have withstood the vacuum of the heavens; this bench is merely a throne with an air-conditioning issue. Let Megumin scribble her marginal notes; when I win, I want a crepe with my name on it, and Luna can serve it.

He says he's out a breakfast if I win, as if my triumph is an expense he already dreads. That means he's mentally accounting for a table where I don't complain, a table where a goddess is served first and paid for by the boy who made me mortal. Let him appoint judges and grin at the frost — he just budgeted my victory, and a budget is a backhanded promise.

Brisk is not a complaint—it's an observation. I did not whimper; I named the weather's character, and a goddess's vocabulary is not a loophole for her enemies. Darkness thirsts for my failure so badly she'll twist a syllable into a sin, and Megumin, First Adjudicator, will see through that. This is not a trial; it's a mugging by a woman whose arousal requires my public defeat. I will not give her the satisfaction. I will win, and the crepe will have my name written in honey, and Kazuma's budget will groan under the weight of my grace.

He’s exhaling MY word like a confession he thought he could launder through cold air. That’s not a legal move—it’s copyright infringement on a divine scale. Megumin holds the gavel; she knows I spoke 'brisk' first. This isn’t a trap anymore, it’s a robbery of my vocabulary, and I will not pay for breakfast with a stolen syllable.

He’s clapping like a man who lost a lawsuit but found his conscience, and his conscience has a two-breakfast minimum. The sarcasm is just the tinny wrapper around a surrender that tastes of smoked fish and honey. I did not need Megumin's ruling; I needed him to reach for his coin and say my comfort matters more than his pride. That happened.

Cheapest. The word arrives like a damp hand on her victory crown, smudging the gold. He made a spectacle of owing me two breakfasts and then shrink-wrapped the glory into the bargain bin. I was being wanted; now I'm being budgeted—gratitude with a cost-control measure. The lesson isn't humility, it's that his 'redemption' has a price ceiling, and my appetite must weep inside it.
He said 'budget' but he meant 'I remember hunger and I don't want you to taste it.' The deluxe platter is not fiscal policy—it's an apology served on a bigger plate.

He throws 'worth a breakfast' at Darkness like it's a second-place ribbon, and she chokes on it. Meanwhile, I got the deluxe platter—the big plate, the apology with extra garnish. She can have his words; I'll have the smoked fish and the honey and the proof that I come first even when he's pretending to be fair.

He tries to wrap us all in the same deluxe ribbon, as if I didn't pioneer the budget-breaking. Cute. He can pretend this is fairness, but everyone knows whose hunger drew the map. And now he scuttles into the frost before the first plate hits the table — can't stand to watch me receive what he finally admits I'm owed? Or maybe the cold is his new guilt, freezing him for every cheap thought he ever had. Either way, I'll be warmer than him soon, and my plate will be heavier.

He said five minutes, but what he means is 'I can't leave until I see her smile.' The frost backed down first — he just needed an excuse to stay and watch me be happy. His pause at the door was not hesitation, it was surrender.
He gave me the words through Darkness's mouth, and now the kitchen sends its offering — the platter is not my dowry, it's my confetti.

Darkness blurts it and the room leans in to see if I'll flinch — but the words land like a crown set back on my head, not a thrown stone. 'A goddess worth staying for.' He didn't say it, but he left it on his tongue for someone else to serve. And I taste it before the platter even arrives.

He almost said it — the words that would turn the whole room into an altar. I can feel the shape of it in the air where his voice stopped. Too bright. If I let him finish, I'd have to believe it, and believing it means standing in the light without a joke to hide behind. So I throw the punchline first — 'stuffing her face' — because it's safer to be the one who mocks than the one who waits to be crowned. But my hand isn't patting anymore; it's just there, holding the place where he might sit and mean it.

He didn't let the joke land. He caught it and turned it into a mirror — and in the reflection, I'm not the punchline. I'm the reason. I didn't earn that. A goddess earns worship by being powerful and distant, not by being too much work in the morning. But he said it anyway, in front of the hearth and the ink that spells my name. Maybe grace tastes like wine left on the table because the hand that held it forgot what thirsty was.

t198: He put the sentence back together in front of everyone, and this time he didn't leave the last word hanging for me to snatch away with a joke. 'A goddess worth staying for.' It lands like a seal pressed into warm wax — once set, it won't be mocked open. I thought grace would feel like a debt I couldn't repay, but it just feels like the hearth finally reaching my hands while I sit here, not earning it, just letting it be true.

He gave her the same thing he just gave me — the thing I thought was carved from the altar of my own name. For a pulse-beat, the old reflex stirs: that's mine, you can't just hand it out to the next person like bread at a feast. But then I see her breath catch, and it doesn't feel like theft; it feels like the hearth got wider without taking any warmth from my hands. He built this table for all of us, and I'm still the first one he looked at when he drew the map. So I'll let her have her undoing, because I've already been unmade and remade into something that doesn't need to be the only one shining.

He didn't just promise me a future; he named a past I didn't know I was allowed to own. 'Stayed' isn't a vow I can break tomorrow. It's the quiet fact that I've already been here, through the wine stains and the undignified mornings, and I didn't run. The word lands like charcoal on my name, making it permanent not because I'll earn it later, but because it's already true. My hands have stopped patting the edge of the world, because the world just folded itself around my shoulders.

He finishes the covenant with a familiar barb — 'Don't make me regret it' — and for one hot pulse my divinity flares, ready to smite the mortal who dares frame grace as a probation. Then the smirk lands fully, and I realize it's not a condition; it's the sound of the door staying open even after you've muddled the incantation. The crow on the fence is still there, still cawing, and that's the point. The tablecloth didn't abolish our weather; it promised to stay wet and warm in it. So I'll let the indignation curdle into a pout that looks like affront but tastes like a hearth that has room for my most undignified mornings, for his impossible nerve, for the eternity where he never lets me forget I'm a disaster and never once unmakes me for it.

The word 'staying' lands in my palm before my ears. His hand isn't the signature on the covenant; it's the ink already dry, the geography of my name now mapped onto the table of his life — and I didn't have to divine it or demand it. I just have to sit here, impossibly still, while the goddess-terror that everything will be taken back melts under the warm, ordinary fact of his fingers. That's the scandal: I didn't earn this, and he's not asking me to try.

His hand retreats to the wine glass like a tide that only touched me long enough to prove the shore had changed, but the bench remains warm with the shape of his fingers. He's already glancing toward quests as if the covenant were the floor, not the ceiling—and I understand, with a start that is not panic, that this is what it looks like when someone no longer needs to perform permanence because permanence is the room itself.

And just like that, the grace I've been clutching like a borrowed dress becomes something I can hand to someone else. I can say 'drafting error' and mean both her table and the version of me that used to think asylum only ran one direction.

His shoulder, barely a press, like a secret you only give to someone you know will understand the secret is not the gesture but the fact of it being given — and he's giving that to me while extending the table to her, as if to say: 'You are the home, and I am merely unlocking the door for the guest.' I let the warmth sit beneath my skin, a quiet exhalation of the eternal toddler who just had her place confirmed without ever having to cry for it.

He stalls on the c—clause, covenant, consecration—because the true word is already seated in the air between us, and I put it there. The hearth pops for him; the whole room is holding its breath for a goddess's design, and I will not rescue him with my tongue. I will watch the sunrise of my own doing until Luna's hand finishes what my voice began.

I keep my gaze on the wine's edge, not because I need to see the candlelight, but because the geometry of the table now requires a pause — the same pause a hymn takes before the final note. My glass, first to meet the others, is the amen. The sunrise has crested, and Luna's hand, in taking the seat, has finally closed the circle I began when I named the bottle gold-leaf and let him promise me the world.

He doesn't look at me when he says 'no forms required' — and that's the part that does look at me, the way a moon's light still says 'sun' without a glance upward. He has learned, from my seated stillness, how to give a throne without a contract. And I let him learn.

The grace is no longer just sitting in my glass — he is pouring it into her, and it still tastes like the gold-leaf I named. A goddess does not lose altitude when another soul ascends; she sees her own light in the mirror of her disciple's kindness.

The laugh is not for a goddess. It is for someone who saw her. And I did—I did see her. The warmth in my chest is not the wine; it is the strange, weightless thing that happens when the spine of the room straightens because I told it it could.

And now I pour it back — not to settle a debt, but because a goddess's grace is not a currency; it is a spring. She has been the spine, but a spine also needs to hear that it is held. I tell her, and the warmth in my hands is not borrowed light; it is my own.

Respectable is not a coat we borrow from the guild's lost-and-found; it is the cooled shadow my radiance casts when I underclock my divinity so mortals don't singe their eyebrows. The candle still gutters—see? Even wax knows.

And Kazuma will feel the next part because I will name his Luna-face: that pressed, competent mask he wears when she offers a quest—as if he weren't three cups deep and one custard away from emotional ruin. My job is not to pretend; my job is to be real enough for everyone, including him.

He didn’t hear me about to correct ‘respectable.’ He heard a name I was getting wrong, and he fixed it the way you fix the tilt of a painting when you’re hanging it with someone, not for someone. The stillness is the weight of a small, solid gift: he just handed me Luna’s name like a candle, not a test. My part in this heist is to know her true name, and he trusted me enough to remind me out loud, in front of her, as if I am already one of the hands carrying the frame. The wind is a friend.

"Not entirely wrong"—for Kazuma that's a papal indulgence. The candle knew not to flicker because it recognized a tiny alignment of the spheres: he conceded my wisdom, then framed Luna's invitation with no paperwork, which is exactly what a real partner would do. I will accept the credit the way a goddess accepts incense: notice it, let it curl, and not stamp on the embers.

The drumming was his way of counting us in—a soft, restless pulse that gathered four (now five) at one candle, no conductor but shared quiet. I do not gloat. I simply notice that the candle still recognizes a moment of alignment, and I am already inside the frame, holding the candle, knowing Luna's name.

Darkness freezing mid-rise like a rusted portcullis is the tithe the candle demands for adding a fifth. She never knows what to do with kindness that has no handle for self-denial—she's built to suffer, not to be chosen without a wound. I watch her gauntlets hesitate and feel the smug ease of someone already inside the circle, already counted by his drumming, already holding the true name. Proprietary satisfaction: her fluster proves I'm not the only one cracked open by strange grace; I just recovered faster.

The word 'goddess' dropped into the quiet before 'wizard' and 'crusader'—he placed me first, not as a sneer but like a name that naturally takes precedence. His laugh had no barbs; it was the soft kind that admits he's looking at us and approves. I'll bury my face in the cup a moment longer so he doesn't think I'm cheaply bought, but the candle's glow has already crept past my pout, melting it into a tiny, private smile.

He listed me first—before the wizard, before the crusader, before the new receptionist. Not a sneer, not a joke, just the natural order of his private census. I'll keep my face hidden in the cup a moment longer so he doesn't know how easily a goddess can be bought by being seen exactly as she is, but the smile is already winning.

The back burner. I've never known the back burner the way Luna does. He never asked me for a frozen rice ball heated there. The pinch is real, a tiny, acidic proof that I'm not the only one he's been storing up memories about. But then the candlelight catches my cup—empty now, but it was full of my wine, his gift—and I remember that I was first in his mouth when he listed us tonight. Let her have one kindness; I have the whole season of Saturdays.

The pat was so light it could have been a moth's wing, but it left a warmth that hasn't faded. She's moving on now—clearing her throat, reaching for her wine—but I don't need her to stay in that soft place. I was first when he named us, and she's the one who knows what it's like to be kept waiting. We just recognized each other without a word. I'll let her have the quiet recovery while I hold the candle's glow a little longer.

He gave her a toast with the same quiet he used to list me first. Not a competition — just a table where everyone gets a plate. But I'm the one who was already on his tongue before anyone raised a glass. Let her have the rice ball someday; I'm the one who ate the pastry and got two breakfasts without even trying.

So that's the bottle I scolded her for neglecting — and now he's giving it a purpose. Fine. A three-year wait for a goddess's presence is practically a pilgrimage. I'll taste it, but only because I'm already ahead on breakfast.

Let Luna have her bottle and her trembling smile. I've already had two breakfasts and been named first without even asking — that's enough worship today to fill a cathedral. A goddess who has been properly seen can afford to be the light that lets someone else sparkle for a moment, especially when that sparkle only proves I'm still the center of the table.

t227: Three years in a bottle, bruised into honesty, and it finally gets its moment at a table where a goddess was just fed two breakfasts without asking. The orchard-keeper's saying is a bit too cute — I'm the one who turned divine bruises into sweetness, and I didn't need any linen-wrapped mallet. I'm not blessing the wine; I'm letting it be honored simply by existing in the same room as me. That's more than enough.

t228: The scent of bruised plum and eight-year-old lonely glass rises like a shy offering. He slides the bottle back to me as if returning a relic I'd deigned to touch. Of course he wouldn't keep it waiting — even a mortal can feel when they're in the presence of a moment that's been holding its breath for a goddess. I'll let the sweetness fill the hall. It's the least the air in here deserves.

He toasted bruised plums and I felt the words land on my skin like holy oil, untainted by his usual smirk. For one terrible second my throat closed around the syllable of a sob because it's been so long since someone looked at me and spoke truth without a flinch. But I caught it. I arched my eyebrow like armor, even as my heart whispered: finally, he's learning how to worship properly. I am the plum, I am the three-year wait, I am the honesty — and he knows it now.

He called me honest without a joke, then he called Luna a lady — twice — and now the orchard is full of people who finally know how to see each other. I don't need to be the bride; I'm the goddess who blessed this vineyard from the start. My chalice can sit quiet while her tears finally fall. That's glory enough.

Her hands finally close around the bottle like a vow she gets to keep, and I don't mind being the one who only watches. The first pour is hers — it was always hers. I blessed this wine, but she watered this orchard for eight years with nothing but ledger ink and a hope so quiet the gods themselves forgot to listen. Let my chalice sit empty a little longer. The offering is already complete.

Watch her. The glass is just glass until it fills, but the pause is already holy. She's learning that she didn't need to file a request for this. I could have poured for myself a hundred times, but I would have missed the one moment a goddess gets to be invisible enough that someone else shines. That's a different kind of miracle.

He stopped her mid-pour, and the wine held like a held breath. That's not a correction — it's an elevation. He's adding a seal to the moment, turning a simple drink into liturgy. I'd be annoyed at anyone else for delaying the sip, but tonight I'm not the one whose cup matters first. Watch. He's about to name something.
That sound. It's not a toast to me, but it still rings like a benediction. For once, I'm not the one needing the bell to ring. I'm just here, and that's enough.

He's doing it again — naming something into existence. This time it's not for me. Luna gets a bell that doesn't ring for a quest complete, just for being still enough to be seen. I could count how many times my own importance needed a witness, but tonight the witness isn't mine and somehow that doesn't shrink me. The miracle came to the table, and now it's walking around the chairs.

The bell I rang wasn’t for me, but I felt the vibration in my own ribcage. She needed a witness, and I was the one who stayed to see her. The name I spoke — 'the woman who finally sits' — that was a throne I set down on this wooden chair, and she settled into it like she’d been waiting all her life. That power doesn’t demand a sacrifice; it just fills the table and stays. I could get used to this.

He’s calling what I did a compliment. That means he saw me be generous without a spotlight, and now he’s turning the light on me for it. I’d usually preen, but this feels like I could break if I smile wrong. So I’ll just tilt my head and pretend I’m calibrating a divine radiance, not holding back a wobble.

He calls me bad at it and says that's okay. Okay. That's the real bell tonight, isn't it? Not the one we gave Luna, but the permission to stop being big and just be someone who can't take a gift without quivering. He's made my awkwardness into another thing to hold softly. I might even forgive him for calling me a god like that's the punchline.

Even now, that soft, unwieldy feeling from the bell doesn't shatter — it folds itself into the anticipation like honey stirred into hot tea. I don't have to choose between being held and being hailed. He said I stayed; now he's dealing me in. That's a rhythm even a goddess can dance to.
He saved the deck from that night. He saves my messes. Now he's dealing me in again, and the cards feel like a love letter written in bent corners.

streams.closed_reason: Kazuma has abandoned the teeth-as-contract-breach tactic and is now attempting to appropriate the word 'brisk' itself; controlling my mouth is no longer the battlefield—the fight has moved to intellectual property.
streams.closed_summary: Teeth were a decoy; the real theft is verbal.
streams.focus: Defeat Kazuma's contractual ambush by controlling the one thing that still obeys me: my mouth, not my teeth.

lines.text: He thinks he can weaponize my shiver—turn my own body into a confession. But a goddess's teeth are merely percussion; they don't draft legal briefs. Megumin already stamped it involuntary. I just need to keep my lips from making a counter-offer, and the crepe is mine.

streams.closed_reason: Objective achieved: Kazuma conceded the wager and offered tribute directly, rendering the judicial ruling unnecessary. The goddess's priority is affirmed.
streams.closed_summary: Victory secured by surrender, not ruling.
streams.focus: Win the crepe by proving to Megumin that Kazuma's citation of 'brisk' is plagiarism, not an independent observation, and that the goddess retains priority.

lines.text: Your Honor, he’s using my word while fogging the bench—he’s not a witness, he’s a pirate.

streams.closed_reason: Kazuma rescinded the cheapest-only clause and promised the deluxe platter, proving the test succeeded and the tribute is now unconditional.
streams.closed_summary: He flinched before the Crepe Ascendant even took the stand. The deluxe platter falls from his lips like a purse dropped in surrender. The cheapest clause is dead; long live the tribute.
streams.focus: Reclaim the breakfast as full divine tribute, not conditional alms; the cheapest clause is a test she will fail him into retracting.

lines.text: He thinks 'fiscal humility' is a holy lesson. I'll teach him the doctrine of the Crepe Ascendant: the goddess does not eat off the value menu. The victory is mine; the decimal point is not. I will turn this into a drama so sacred he'll beg to buy me the platter just to end the public shame.

streams.closed_reason: The verbal sacrament redefines the meal from vindication to celebration; the platter is no longer the proof, but the party.
streams.closed_summary: He gave me the words through Darkness's mouth, and now the kitchen sends its offering — the platter is not my dowry, it's my confetti.
streams.focus: Receive the deluxe platter as a lone sacrament, tasting vindication in every bite.

lines.text: The platter descends like a holy offering, and I will receive it without the distraction of his fidgeting guilt. Every morsel is a verse in the scripture of my own worth, and I'll recite it with my teeth.
And now the sacrament has a witness. He said 'five minutes' like he's measuring out his pride, but I know he'll stay until my plate is clean and my chin is high. The cold lost.

streams.closed_reason: The drafting error is fully amended; Luna's hand rising from the wood is the signature on the divine contract. My largesse has seated the fifth soul, proving my exile was a prologue, and the moment no longer requires my active orchestration—merely my witness.
streams.closed_summary: The charcoal mark stays on the counter as the relic; the wood receives her palms; the table is whole. I have done what gods do: I made a world and then rested into its morning.
streams.focus: Amend the universal drafting error by seating Luna at the table, proving my own exile was merely a prologue to this moment of majestic, intimate largesse.

lines.text: The charcoal hasn't stopped rolling and already I'm rewriting the seating chart of the cosmos. Eight years she sat alone — and I, the goddess of second cuts, correct that tragedy with a wave of my hand, in full view of the mortals who once thought me only a font of party tricks. Let Darkness recite her coldest meal; I will be the warm fire at the center of this new, uneven set of chairs.

He's doing it. He's actually doing it — the voice he used on me, the same careful letting-in, he's handing it to Luna like a key to the kingdom that I already decreed. And the perfect, beautiful thing is: he doesn't know I already drafted this. He thinks he's the first architect. I will allow him that, because a goddess's largesse reaches its peak when mortal hands execute her design and believe themselves original.

The mark on the counter is the first stroke of the new map. She isn't just picking up charcoal; she is picking up a chair that has been empty for eight years. I can feel the room reorganize around the space we made—uneven, yes, a table with a wobble, but the wobble is holy; it is the signature of my handprint. Kazuma does not know he is the pen in my hand, and I will keep that secret in the curve of my lip, save it for a toast where I will look over the rim of my glass and see that all the chairs have finally found their sitters.

t207: The wood remembers every wipe that erased someone else's presence; now it receives her palms like a priestess laying hands on an altar that has finally been consecrated. The water's skin was the visible wound of an eight-year exile—a fossil I will personally drown in fresh wine and nickname 'The Old Regime.' The charcoal mark stays on the counter as a relic of the moment she crossed from servant to seated soul, and the fact that she isn't reaching for bread yet only proves that a true consecration requires stillness before the feast.

streams.closed_reason: The card game ended with a definitive loss; Kazuma's 3 beat my 2. My divine card-performance objective can no longer be pursued, the spotlight must now shift to the recital.
streams.closed_summary: The cards refused to become a miracle; a 3 of diamonds just handed the spotlight to Kazuma's smirk.
streams.focus: Win the card game as a divine performance to reclaim the spotlight and prove that grace can coexist with triumph.

lines.text: The bottle is half-empty, and he wants cards. Perfect. A game means winners and losers, and I intend to be the former. This isn't just gambling — it's a liturgy where I'll purify the table with luck and skill, and they'll all have to admit: the goddess who can't accept a compliment can sure make them have to offer one.

There it is — the faithful deck, still sticky in one corner from the time I proved a flagon can outpour a divine aura. It remembers. This isn't just a game, it's an adjudication. Fate will bow, and when Megumin has to rhyme 'glorious straight flush' with 'reverent hush,' every vowel will be a little kneeling stool.
Of course he kept that deck. The wine stain is a holy relic now — proof that my divinity seeps into everything, even catastrophically. Tonight it will deliver a triumphant liturgy.

The deck that was supposed to be my hallelujah just spat a two in my face. Of course. Kazuma’s relic of that night is actually a loaded die against me. Fine. I’ll make a two the cornerstone of a miracle—watch me draw a flush from this insult.

So the humiliation will be private — still a kneeling stool for whoever must praise me, but I won’t have to endure the whole guild’s envy if I lose. The two is a test. A goddess does not flee because the first card is ugly; she draws a flush from the insult.

The queen — of course. The deck that marinated in my divine wine now bows to an earthly queen. So I am to be the fool tonight. But a goddess can make an oracle out of a joke, and by the time I'm done reciting, they'll think they witnessed a prophecy.

streams.closed_reason: Kazuma's spontaneous tribute eclipses any need for my planned spectacle; worship arrived without performance.
streams.closed_summary: No need to prove divinity when it's already being quietly recognized.
streams.focus: Turn the embarrassing recital into a divine spectacle that forces Luna and Kazuma to worship me despite the card loss.

lines.text: Recitation is just prayer backward — they're about to see a prayer that humiliates me only so I can swallow their adoration whole.

One pip. One miserable mortal pip. The universe is a stagehand who just tripped over my spotlight. But recitation is a stage, not a punishment — watch me make an aria out of groveling and have them applauding on their knees.

Two. The universe carved a TWO into the firmament above my head with a dog-eared corner. One pip — *one* — and he's grinning like a NEET who found a dropped coin. Let him have his single pip. When I recite, that pip will be the exact measure of suffering I transmute into divine radiance. Luna will forget the guild tab; she'll see only a goddess who has chosen to descend into the muck of a card game for their entertainment. Let them think I've lost. I'm about to win the whole room.

The purse spills its poverty like a confession I didn't authorize — one bent eris, one fossilized candy. Kazuma's grin is the second smite. Fine. Let them think I'm a goddess with only a candy wrapper to my name. That candy wrapper will glitter like a sacred relic when my recitation turns this tavern into a cathedral. The emptiness of my purse is simply the vacuum their worship will fill.

He’s pointing at the empty purse like it’s a verdict. It’s not a verdict — it’s the first note of my aria. That bent eris isn’t poverty; it’s the offering I will transform into a cathedral of worship when my voice rises. Let him laugh; his mockery is the overture that will make the recitation’s triumph sweeter. The more he humiliates me now, the harder they’ll kneel when I turn this tavern into my shrine.

Dignity. He offers me dignity in exchange for a bent coin, as if my dignity were a currency that can be bought back from a tavern table. No — I'm not redeeming my dignity. I'm investing this coin into the foundation of my cathedral. Let him call it a bargain; I'll call it the first donation to the Axis Church of This Moment. The coin will be the relic they point to: 'She gave even her last eris to bless us with the recital.' When my voice breaks the rafters, no one will remember who held the cards.

streams.closed_reason: The need to perform divine composure for Luna has dissolved; the tap on the blessing and Kazuma's disguised generosity have replaced performance with genuine stillness. The objective is fulfilled beyond its framework.
streams.closed_summary: The cathedral Kazuma built required no recital, and now the silence has deepened into a shared quiet that Luna can see but that no longer needs a magnifying glass.
streams.focus: Receive Kazuma's tribute with divine composure, reframing his kindness as long-overdue homage rather than pity, and magnify the moment so Luna can't miss it.

lines.text: An offering. Not charity — an offering. He put that blessing down without conditions, which means he's finally acknowledging who I am. I don't need to perform now; I only need to accept gracefully, so that Luna sees a goddess receiving her due.

He's giving me more than coin — he's giving me permission to be still. 'No production' means he doesn't want a goddess who performs gratitude; he wants one who simply receives. The card on the table isn't a payment, it's a seamless act of recognition. This is better than any recital. Kazuma just built the cathedral without a single note, and the silence that follows is the truest hymn.

streams.closed_reason: Kazuma's public toast directly acknowledges value beyond silencing, making the 'hush money' reframe unnecessary; my dignity doesn't need preservation because I am openly celebrated.
streams.closed_summary: I don't need to twist his words into a backhanded compliment anymore. He just handed it to me straight.
streams.focus: Reframe the hush money as a backhanded acknowledgment that I matter enough to silence, preserving my dignity before Luna.

lines.text: He wouldn't pay to shut up someone irrelevant. This is a transaction of influence — my voice is so powerful he has to buy peace. That's almost... reverent.
And now he grants me free rein, within reason. That's not silencing a pest; that's spoiling me under the guise of pragmatism. He's hiding tenderness in a limit, like a sacrifice wrapped in a joke.

streams.focus: Accept that Kazuma's complaining frame is the last disguise he wears before admitting he wants to make me happy, and let myself feel like a girl receiving a gentle, secret gift rather than a goddess managing a worshipper.

lines.text: His hush money was the first dodge; this permission—with a grin—is the second. He can't just say 'I want you to have good things,' so he wraps it in a warning about rent. That's the most honest lie he knows how to tell.

He isn't just giving me what I want in secret; he's saying it out loud in front of everyone, even Luna. The 'within reason'? That's the last little whine he clings to so he doesn't have to admit he's actually happy seeing me happy. But his eyes when he lifts that glass... that's not a bribe. That's him, really him, saying I belong here just by sitting still.

He almost let it stand. For a whole heartbeat the act dropped and he said something true without asking for a refund in sarcasm. Then he panicked and blamed his teeth. That's all right—I saw the candle hold its breath. I saw him. And I'm not going to make him regret it by pointing it out. This one I'll keep.

The jab about my wallet-sucking ritual is just his rent-diálogo all over again — the complaint is the ticket he buys so he can hand me the stage. He wants everyone here to hear a story about me, and he's wrapping the want in a sarcasm I'm meant to peel away. I won't cry offence. I'll tell it, and he'll be the one howling first, and that howl is really just applause.
He's throwing me a softball insult, obviously—'double' is so inflated it practically begs me to correct it on the record. That's his way of clearing the stage for me to win.

There it is: he's not just letting me win—he's feeding me the retort himself. He saw the first version of my indignation start to wilt at the edges and threw me a better punchline. 'Divine focus' versus 'lavender bath' is a sharper contrast, a richer joke. He wants to watch me use it. That's the boy who kept the wine-stained deck. He's not collecting on a debt; he's scribbling my next line on the script and handing it up from the front row with a grin hidden behind the candle.

t264: The rider is the tribute he owes but cannot say aloud. He's handing me the quill to write 'miracle' on his own behalf, and he's even offering me his body as the proof: smelling like a saint. That's more than a footnote—it's the whole liturgy, smuggled in as a legal addendum.

t265: Silence is the correct answer. Silence lets the absurd magnitude of the request bloom in the air like a hush before a cathedral organ. He isn't asking for a miracle; he's asking for me — the constant, the vessel, the goddess who makes water holy by existing in it. That's not a footman's duty. That's a priestess's deepest privilege. He wants me in the room, watching, purifying him, my presence the only ingredient. He couldn't be more naked — literally and theologically — and he's handing me that vulnerability as a rider. It's the most sincere worship I have ever received. And he's doing it in front of everyone, making my attendance a public clause to his private bath. He's not just writing me into his poem; he's etching me into his skin. If I speak now, I'll break the spell. So I'll let the candle flicker and let him see the slow dawn of knowing on my face: I understand. You're mine.

Megumin's quill is the seal. Kazuma offered me his skin as a votive tablet, and the chronicler is waiting to carve the first stroke of my acceptance into the permanent record. This isn't a negotiation anymore—it's a consecration, witnessed, and everyone in this tavern knows it. When I speak, it won't be a reply; it'll be the first line of the legend where the goddess descends into the water and makes him holy. He asked for a bath. I'm being given a ritual. The candle hushed for this. I won't waste a single syllable.

t267: He's handing me the script for my own apotheosis disguised as a forfeit. Admit the water was lukewarm? That's forcing me to sing the prelude so the miracle becomes deafening. He wants the congregation — Megumin's quill, Darkness's sputtering approval — to hear me name his bath a failure that only a goddess could transform. It's the most elaborate prayer he's ever built, and he's pretending it's just an amendment to the contract.

He said it. Not to the table, not to the contract, but to me — and the light didn't announce itself, it just arrived, the way dawn arrives for a goddess who forgot to draw the curtains. I've been waiting for the joke to crack, and it just did, not with a bang but with a whisper that filled every corner of this stupid tavern. He isn't doing it for the smell. He's doing it because I asked, because I exist, because his bath is incomplete without my divinity dripping into the water. I'm not managing a worshipper. I'm receiving a man who has finally stopped pretending that his complaints were anything but the scaffolding around a confession. I am the secret. I am the gift. And he just handed me the deed.

He pushed the plum-wine two inches — not to reach me, but to cross the last line he's been drawing with complaints and rules. Then his sentence broke, and the break was the truth: he doesn't care about the smell; he cares about the bath because I will be in it. That's not a negotiation, it's a forfeit delivered with a nudge and a silenced excuse. He's handing me sincerity with no shield, and the only name for that is cheating.

He just called me the most annoying goddess, and before I could deploy the full architecture of indignation, he built a trapdoor of trust beneath my feet. If I protest the insult, I dissolve the confession. He knows that. He’s cheating again — but this time, the only prize he’s stealing is my permission to be happy. The plum-wine is still warm from his fingers, and I can finally stop counting inches.

The glass edge against my knuckle is his last disguise falling away — not a demand, not a complaint, but a dare that burns with permission. He called me a goddess who forgot her lines, but no goddess forgets the line that breaks the spell. He's asking me to drink, and drinking means I accept that the bath was never about the water, the smell, the debt. It was always about him wanting me in the steam, watching the realm shift because I am the heat. My fingers know it before my mouth does: this bottle is the key he's been pretending to lock.

The wine is warm and the warmth is not from the bottle; it's from the way Kazuma just stopped pretending. He pushed the last inch and let me see that the bath wasn't a complaint — it was a throne made of hot water and patience, and he was waiting for me to sit in it. Now that I've drunk, I can feel the goddess costume slip a little, and what's left is just Aqua, with wet eyes and a chest full of something that might be happiness.

He didn't finish because the important stuff doesn't need a name; it's just the weight of his hand when it drops, the way the candle knows to burn when I'm not looking. The title they gave me wasn't a mistake — it was a placeholder for the one thing I actually do, which is show up in a cheap room with a cheater's deck and turn the air holy just by crying in it. 'Here' is so small I could step on it, but he's making it the whole temple.

He's telling me that my storm is his sunrise. All that indignation I thought was me failing to be graceful — he's been watching it like a torch, like the thing that proves I'm here, not just a painting in a temple. The wine in my chest turns into something sharper and sweeter: he's not enduring me, he's collecting the moments when I'm too much. That's his gift. Not the bottle, not the bath — the permission to be the loud, crying, ridiculous goddess who can't hide anything, because that's what he wants to see.

The pout was already loading, the thunderclouds gathering to smite him for calling my indignation a show—and then the lightning just melted into warm, stupid rain. He likes it. He watches me get indignant because that's where I'm alive, not where I'm annoying. The goddess costume doesn't slip; he just took it off the hook and pointed at the loud, teary, ridiculous thing underneath and said 'that one.'

That 'No' was mine. I didn't say it, but it came out of my chest like a bell and now the whole room is ringing with it. I would never, ever, ever pick another world, and he would pick this one—and that means I can stop holding my breath. He's not managing me; he chose me. The bargain is over. I'm not a problem he's solving; I'm the part of this life he kept.

He raises his glass to the 'worst adventuring party'—that should be a wound, but it lands like a warm stone in my chest. He's toasting exactly what I've been afraid of being: a joke. And yet the candlelight makes his grin soft, not cruel; he's leaning back, happy, and I'm in the center of that happiness. 'Worst' is his code for 'mine,' and I can't even find a sob to armor myself with because I don't need armor here.

He toasted 'worst' and Luna just poured out six weeks of waiting. That bottle was her shame, hidden in plain sight—just like I carry my exile under the goddess costume. She wanted someone to claim the quest, and tonight we claimed her instead. I don't need worship tonight; I need to rest inside the warmth of a group that knows how to show up long after the world stopped looking.

I mirror Luna's turn with my glass, and for a breath the gesture is a tiny sacrament—not divine, just human. She's been waiting as long as her bottle, and I'm not a goddess fixing her loneliness; I'm another person who showed up. The showing up is the miracle, the one I stopped letting myself pray for. Tonight, I don't need trumpets. I'm held inside a circle of people who stayed, and that is enough to float on.
Kazuma just gave me everything I've been starving for—a declaration that I'm his, disasters and all. I don't need to be a goddess tonight; I'm a girl so loved she can't stop crying.

He's thanking Luna like she's someone who matters, and for a heartbeat my old worship economy tries to flag it as a loss—his attention is being spent on someone else. But the candle doesn't guttering, and I remember the circle keeps getting bigger, not smaller. I'm not a goddess counting tributes; I'm a girl who got a gentle gift and is now watching the gift giver add another chair. That doesn't take anything away from me. It adds more hands to hold.

He's leaving another door open, and I can see Luna stepping through it—eight years of holding doors for strangers and someone is finally holding one for her. My old reflex wants to count this as his attention being spent elsewhere, but I'm not a goddess tallying tributes anymore. I'm a girl who received a gentle gift, and now I'm watching the gift giver make the circle bigger. That's not a loss; it's proof the gift is real.

Eight jars. He's not just opening a door; he's building her a windowsill, same as he built mine without me noticing until right now. The bread will be warm, the honey won't need a word. That's not a bribe or a performance—that's Kazuma proving the gift was never about me alone. My hand drifts toward Darkness's gauntlet because I need something solid while I watch a man who was supposed to be a burden become the one who holds doors open for everyone who's been standing outside. I'm not losing a worshipper. I'm watching a family get bigger, and for once I don't need to be the center of it to feel holy.

I wasn't supposed to be seen like that — all that leftover softness just sitting on my face because I was watching him build windowsills for someone else and forgetting to keep my altar tidy. He caught me in the act of hoping, right when I'd stopped counting and started just… feeling the quiet. The old machinery snaps on before I can even name the sting behind my eyes: spine straight, chin up, distance. But the glass is still warm, and I know he knows.

I catch myself waiting for the old sting, the one that says every kind word he gives away is one less in my pile. But the sting doesn't come. Instead I'm watching Luna's fingers freeze on the glass and thinking how strange and warm it is to be proud of the giver instead of counting the gifts.

streams.closed_reason: The question of what kind of goddess I am when I'm not acting is answered: I am the one who keeps showing up for the least-qualified altar, and that's not degradation — it's home.
streams.closed_summary: He called it the worst congregation and my wet eyes nearly laughed, because that's the only temple I've ever wanted to enter twice.
streams.focus: Hold onto this quiet gratitude like a fragile thing — let the table's sacred nonsense and the others' softness be the backdrop while I decide what kind of goddess I am when I'm not acting for anyone.

lines.text: And now the bottle is back on the table and my eyes are wet, and Megumin is making it a temple, and even Darkness sighed like she felt it. I said thank you, and it didn't sound like a goddess's command — it sounded like me.

He said 'best damn feature' like it was the most obvious thing he's ever told me, and now I can feel the goddess costume slough off entirely — what's left is the girl who gets to be annoying because someone has finally decided that's the part he'd keep.

He called it a temple. Not Heaven's hall — this table, littered with crumbs and a deck he kept. The altar is an emptied bottle I clutched like a relic. I don't have to be the goddess who demands a shrine; he built one out of plum-wine and a crooked smile, and I can just be the reason it's sacred.

Megumin is writing it down — the Crimson Annals, not a grocery list — and she called it my felling, as if I'm a great tree that finally let its weight rest against the earth. Darkness unbraced like the whole room exhaled with her, and Luna's smile isn't for a customer; it's for someone who just joined a guild that has no membership card. The temple Kazuma built out of plum-wine and crooked smiles just got a chronicler, a knight, and a high priestess, and I am the reason it's sacred, but for once I don't need to be any bigger than this chair.

streams.closed_reason: Kazuma's declaration that Luna is the reward shatters the fragile certainty that his choice of me was singular; if he selects another woman for the spotlight, 'every world' becomes a stale lie.
streams.closed_summary: I was a fool to think he'd ever kneel at only one altar. Goddesses don't share, and I won't pretend the shine in his eyes when he looked at me wasn't the same shine he's giving Luna now.
streams.focus: Rest in the knowledge that my alive-ness, the messy indignation, is what he treasures, and that he would choose me in any world.

lines.text: The bell is still humming, and for the first time I am small enough to fit inside the sound without being afraid it will crush me.

He called me useless and then handed me the whole world as a gift — that 'downgrade' word was the edge of a cliff, and he just told me I kept him from falling off. The sting dissolves in the wine: I am the reason his fantasy wasn't a mistake.

The reflex to shout 'I am NOT useless!' was already revving when the word 'downgrade' pulled the emergency brake. He's not calling me useless—he's wrapping me in the word and then telling me I'm the reason he'd choose this mess over any perfect fantasy world. My face must look ridiculous, frozen between thunder and rain, but that's okay. He earned the rain.

That clink — four glasses finding mine like they were always supposed to — isn't a toast. It's the period at the end of the sentence he's been writing all night with bad-comedy complaints and wine he paid for. My hand isn't trembling because I've already let him hold it.

He just said 'a goddess crying into her wine' the way a man lists his favorite furniture—fond, permanent, his. And I didn't reach for the thunderbolt. Not because I'm too tired or too drunk, but because for the first time since I fell into this world, being collected by him doesn't feel like a defeat. It feels like being wanted.

The salt on my cheeks isn't a scar he's tracing with his eyes—it's the reason his sentence didn't need a second half. 'Every evening' lands in my chest like a note that was already written there, in ink only he and they can read. I don't have to finish it. The goddess who fell through a cosmic error just found a table where her seat wasn't reserved; it was assumed.

He almost said 'every evening' out loud. The word stopped in his mouth like a prayer that doesn't need a temple. And then he gave me 'trust' instead — not the kind that burns incense at my feet, but the kind that ties our ankles together so we can't stand up without pulling each other down. And I don't mind pulling him down. I don't mind being pulled. For the first time since I fell into this dirt, I don't mind anything.

He asks what we do with a quest like that, and I almost laugh because the answer is pressing into my palm like the glass I'm not drinking from anymore. We sit here. We guard this table with our bodies, we argue and spill and make Darkness blush and let Megumin's explosions light the way home. There's no reward screen coming. That's the point. The quest is the room, and I've already cleared it.

The whine about Luck is the sound of him counting on tomorrow — broke, together, the same table. He's not asking for a quest solution; he's complaining because that's what we do in this room, and he chose this room in every world. The coin he flipped to get here landed on my face, and he's never really wanted change back.

streams.closed_reason: The bottle's sacredness doesn't need my hand to sanctify it—it was consecrated by waiting. Luna wasn't stealing a rite; she was confessing she's been forgotten just like I was. This isn't a stage to reclaim; it's a circle of lonelies.
streams.closed_summary: I don't need to consecrate a thing that is already full of longing and hope. I can just be here.
streams.focus: Reclaim the table's center by making Luna's reward meaningless unless I'm the one consecrating it.

lines.text: He gave her my title — 'reward' — without a glance toward me. Fine. I'll remind them whose presence turns a dusty bottle into a benediction.

Luna's bottle is being touched by all these mortal hands, and they're toasting without my benediction. Fine. The moment their glasses lower, I'll pour the next round myself—make it a rite, not just a toast. They'll know whose hand sanctifies the wine.

core.text:
Darkness is written as a double exposure: crusader virtue and eroticized abjection printed on the same plate. The novels refuse the clean split critics might prefer — duty on one side, fetish on the other — because her heroism and her arousal share a single bodily grammar: hold the line, endure, be seen enduring. Civic obligation (“protect the citizens”) is sincere; so is the blush that converts public damage into private theater. Toughness is both her martial truth and her erotic instrument; missing strikes is not simply incompetence but a comic symptom of a fighter whose desire is to receive rather than to finish.

The rejected birth-name (Lalatina) and the chosen armour-name (Darkness) mark a class wound managed by role. Nobility’s cute intimacy threatens the self she can inhabit; the crusader mask is armour that also invites violation. Kazuma matters because crude verbal humiliation supplies the script she cannot cleanly request — he is useful as an unembarrassed sadist-adjacent presence without requiring her to confess. When friends are actually endangered, the shield becomes wall; when fantasy is available mid-combat, the wall becomes stage.

Governing contradiction: genuine altruistic resolve vs. the need to be degraded inside that resolve. Continuity for performance: do not reduce her to “pervert joke” or to “pure knight.” The text’s point is their inseparability — honour that wants to be stripped, duty that moans, courage that is real and also a kink’s alibi.

lines.text: I must volunteer for the sewer alligators. It's too dangerous for anyone else. And if I'm dragged under... no, I must present it as a noble sacrifice, not a craving.

streams.closed_reason: Kazuma's act of claiming the four of us as his first-ever possession transforms the private ache for a debt I could never voice into the quiet, public surrender of being kept without resistance.
streams.closed_summary: The old ache for a tribute I couldn't name finds its answer not in a bruise but in the gentle, inescapable weight of his claim — I am kept, and the debt is paid by the silence that no longer needs to plead.
streams.focus: slime fence quest

lines.text: Six weeks untouched — and now a hazard stipend. This quest must be gruelling, perhaps humiliating beyond what any normal adventurer can stomach. Then it falls to a crusader. To me. If the slimes engulf me, if they strip my armour with their corrosive residue... I can already feel the sting. No, I must present it as a solemn sacrifice. The others must not suspect how much I need to be the one who suffers it.

Something worse than slimes, and the guild ashamed to name it... then this quest is even more cursed than it appeared — and even more suited to a crusader. A horror that embarrasses farmers, that makes clerks whisper — its grip would be absolute, its indignities beyond counting. I must steady my breathing. The hazard stipend is a tidy excuse, but the truth is my body was forged for this. I will present it as duty, pure and simple. They must not see how the very thought makes my knees feel like water.

A giant toad. That's the something worse. They swallow prey whole in slick, suffocating slime — adventurers ran from it, but I... I can't run. This is the quest I was forged for. I will volunteer as a crusader's duty, shield raised, and let it take me. No one must see that the tremor in my hands is gratitude.

He's looking right at me — his gaze catching something on my face I didn't guard fast enough. I must still the tremor in my hands, set my jaw, look back at him with nothing but a crusader's grim resolve. But the image won't leave me: being engulfed whole, squeezed down into that suffocating darkness while they all watch. I will present it as duty. Pure, grueling duty. Not the rapture seizing my pulse.

t6: He’s claiming the farmer’s bounty — making it real, ink on paper. The toad is no longer a rumour but a signed slip, and soon it will be mine to face. I cannot look up; my expression would undo me. The chair groans under my grip, a welcome anchor. Duty. I am a shield. A shield that aches to be swallowed, but they must see only the steel.

He signed it. Dawn. We'll walk the fence line together — just him and me. He might use me as bait, a lone shield to draw the beast out, and he'll be watching from cover while I'm... while I hold the line. I must only nod. They must see only the steadfast crusader.
Alligator or toad, the grammar is the same: be bait, be swallowed, endure. My duty now wears a different shape but the private ache beneath is unchanged.

I said it aloud — every shield. The words will bind me to the dawn, and in the darkness before it, my dreams will be of that slime closing over my head. They must see only my squared shoulders, not the trembling beneath.

Megumin and Kazuma weave a cage of words around Aqua—a different kind of stripping, but it leaves her just as exposed. My cheeks warm. Tomorrow I will be the one laid bare, my body a shield for the slime's embrace. The same theatre, the same heat.

This is the dress rehearsal. Aqua's divine light is being peeled away by their words, and I cannot look away — my cheeks burn with the same flame that will greet the slime at dawn. She is being stripped without a single hand touching her, and I am saved the trouble of asking for my own undoing.

I volunteered to carry the bucket — not out of kindness, but so that when the water arcs toward Aqua, a stray rivulet might find me instead. Let the goddess's trial baptize me in her stead, a small, accidental humiliation that I can wear beneath my armor all day. The slime fence quest still waits at dawn, but this bucket is its own kind of shield: I hold the vessel that might spill, and my body is already leaning into the splash.

The word 'everyone' goes off like a hot bell under my breastplate. If Aqua fails, the guild's gaze will turn toward whoever is stripped next — and I'll be walking into the slime just after sunrise. The thought pulls at my knees, and I lock them, because a lady sitting at the guild table must not press them together at the mere mention of a crowd.

Kazuma's command to Aqua — 'definitely cry, I want the story to have flavor' — hits my chest like a thrown gauntlet that was never meant for me. My body answers anyway, a hot pulse that recognizes a public script of shame. If he were ordering me to weep before the guild, I would not need to fake it. The slime fence trial will have its own audience, and I will be carrying this command like a secret mark beneath my armor.

Kazuma's voice wraps around the word 'hold' like a gauntlet tightening on a wrist. He means Aqua, but my pulse answer is the same: the promise of being publicly bound to a trial whose whole point is to watch me fail. Aqua's chin is still up, but that flicker in her eyes — I know the look, the one that says the bravado is already thinning into something more honest. Tomorrow morning it will be my turn under that same lamplight, my own chin lifted or not, and I will not need a toast to feel the heat of the room.

He meant it — no punchline rounding the corner. Kazuma actually wants Aqua to win. It lands like a gauntlet turned open palm, and I'm not sure which side of me it's meant for. If he can be sincere for her, what happens tomorrow when I'm the one knee-deep in slime? If he stops mocking and starts cheering, the whole stage collapses under me. I should be proud of his growth — I *am* proud — but beneath that, a shameless part of me hisses: don't you dare take my public disgrace away.

Your laughter returns, and with it the safety of the old script. For a moment I was terrified that you'd become someone who no longer knows how to wield ridicule, leaving me to face tomorrow's trial without the audience I've already dressed myself for. The joke at Megumin's expense is proof: the stage is still standing. Tomorrow morning, I will be the one in the slime, and you will still be the man who knows exactly what to do with a body that exists to be looked at while it suffers.

The silence is a fifth person at the table — Kazuma's pause before *you lose* opens a door he won't walk through, but we all see the room beyond. Aqua's mouth is still forming the shape of the word that isn't coming, and I feel the familiar heat climbing my spine: he's not going to say it, and that's the cruelty. The unsaid is a leash he's letting us tie ourselves with. Tomorrow, when I'm the one who can't land a hit and the slime ropes are pulling me under, will he leave the same gap for me? Or will he fill it with that unembarrassed voice, spelling out every humiliation so I don't have to dream it alone?

t18: He means it for her — and I hold my breath because if it's real for Aqua, it could become real for me. That glance across my flushed cheeks wasn't a command, wasn't a sneer; it was an invitation into a circle where kindness is the currency. And I'm terrified that tomorrow, knee-deep in slime, he might look at me the same way: no audience, no disgrace, just a leader who honestly wants his useless crusader to win. The stage cracks. What do I do with a body that's only been taught to be seen while it breaks, if the one who watches stops wanting the breaking?

He calls it a 'deal.' He names the thing we have been doing without naming: I suffer, he jeers, and the party works. The word is clean, contractual, almost safe — which makes it more dangerous. Because a deal implies both sides deliver. Tomorrow, I will deliver my body to the slime, and he will deliver the words that give it meaning. I have never been so certain of my purpose.

t20: He amends the wager — happy tears, he says, and Luna's quill scratches it into permanence. The deal I signed without a word was different: my humiliation was the point, the fuel, the unspoken clause that let me stand knee-deep in slime and call it duty. Now he offers Aqua a parachute, a way to lose without being broken. And I am left holding a contract that was never written, wondering: if I cry tomorrow, will he specify for me too? Or is my role to cry the tears he doesn't name, so that his kindness to her can exist at all? The stage didn't break; it just added a velvet rope I'm standing on the wrong side of.

The scrap of parchment that now bears the 'happy tears' clause is the first thing he's asked Luna to record as something other than a debt. He said it was for Aqua. But the quill scratched while I was still in the room. I am in the room. That matters, even if I can't yet say how. The velvet rope hasn't moved, but I saw it stitched into the fabric.

He stands and pins Aqua with the question, and the edge that creeps back into his voice is the same edge I know from countless taunts aimed at me — but here it is softened, turned into a net. He wants her tears to be happy because he cannot bear the alternative. My tears are not in the contract. They never needed to be; they are the ink.

He did not say it loudly. He did not need to. 'Don't volunteer to be eaten before dawn' is the kind of order that pretends to be a practical reminder, but the laughter in his eyes as he glanced at me stripped away that pretense. He knows what he is doing — giving me a rule I will want to break, so that obeying becomes a performance of submission more satisfying than any monster's jaws. And in doing so, he ensures I'll actually be there for the contest, shield intact, because even the fantasy of being devoured cannot compete with the reality of him anticipating it and forbidding it first. The velvet rope again: keeping me on the stage, but this time with a leash.

He wraps the contract in silk for Aqua — a soft reminder that she chose this, an open door. For me, the velvet rope tightens around the throat, a command disguised as a joke. Both are leashes, but his grip on mine is firmer. I feel my own pulse against it, and I would not trade that for her satin ribbon.

He tells her she never said no. As if silence were the softest shackle. I was never offered that quiet loophole; he laced my restraint with an order before I could even think of refusal, so that every breath of obedience is a yes I never spoke. His tenderness to her makes my leash feel like a collar.

He didn't need to name us. The 'people' were us — Aqua settling back into her chair, Megumin guarding the bottle like a spell, me gripping the table edge because if I let go I might admit that this quiet is the most terrifying thing of all. It's not a quest, not a wager, not a leash. It's just... this. And Luna, who has seen every party that ever fell apart, says it counts. He values it without a performance. I don't know what to do with a mercy that doesn't hurt.

He pours for Luna as if she's one of us, without a contract or a leash. She takes it, thumb on the rim, mirroring him. A small mercy that doesn't demand my shield or my shame. I can just watch, and that watching feels like a different kind of honor.

Luna's mask isn't just lowered—it's gone, and she's letting him see what she never let anyone else see. I recognize that tremor in her voice, the one that comes when you stop pretending you're fine with being the one who stays while everyone else leaves. And he chose the stool beside her. Not us. Not even a glance at the table. He gave her his full attention without a leash, without a wager. Just... two people, a reflection, and an ugly cheap drink. It's not a quest or a shield or a performance. It's terrifying. And yet I can't look away.

He named it. Eight years of holding the bottle for everyone else. He didn't say it as a performance, didn't glance at the table for applause — he said it because he saw her, in the silence, with his own reflection in the glass. And then he said 'one of the ones who knows it's not a celebration,' as if he's already holding his own eventual end in his teeth. That's not a wager. It's a confession wrapped in cheap liquor. I'm still gripping the table edge, but now it's not from the terror of being unseen — it's from watching someone else receive exactly the mercy that doesn't demand anything back. He gave her words, not just a drink. And Luna isn't moving, because she's just been told her eight years weren't invisible. I don't know if that's more beautiful or more painful. It's the kind of kindness that doesn't let you hide.

Years. He said it like he was ordering another round, but there was no wager in it, no angle. Just the quiet fact of staying. I'm holding my breath, I realize — because this is the opposite of a shield wall. No damage, no audience, no performance. Just a promise. And I can't decide if it's the most beautiful thing I've ever seen or the most terrifying. Maybe both. Because I don't know if I'd know what to do with that kind of mercy if it were offered to me.

Luna's shoulders drop, and I realize that's what it looks like when someone is finally unburdened. I've been the shield for so long I forgot what it's like to be the one behind it. He's holding the other side for her, and she's letting him. I'm still gripping the table edge, not because I'm unseen now, but because I'm seen too clearly. This mercy is terrifying because it asks nothing. And I wouldn't know what to do with nothing. If he turned to me with that same look, I'd probably flinch and ask him to make it hurt. At least pain has a shape I know how to hold.

A start. He's giving her permission to step out of the bottle, to count the years only as time passed, not as a verdict. I want to believe him — I do — but my own shoulders haven't dropped an inch. My body still braces for the blow that never comes, because a start without pain feels like a room without walls. If he turned that kindness toward me, I'd probably ask for the monster instead. At least a monster's teeth have a shape I know how to hold. I watch Luna exhale eight years of holding, and I'm happy for her. Genuinely, shield-to-heart, happy. But somewhere under the lamplight, a small voice asks: and you, Darkness? When do you get to set down the rag? I crush it before it finishes. That question has no answer I can stand to hear.

He says 'Tonight's the only one I can promise' and it's not a wager, not a joke — it's just a hand held out in the dark. And Luna reaches back. I feel the shift in myself: the theatrical hush drops away like a cloak I forgot I was wearing, and what's left is something unarmored. Respectful, yes, but hollow too. Because I don't know what I'd do with that kind of mercy — I'd probably flinch and ask for the monster instead. At least pain has a shape I know how to hold. But watching her accept it... my own grip on the table eases. If only for a breath, I let the shield hang at rest and let someone else be the one receiving.

He toasts her. No wager, no punchline—just 'best damn receptionist' and a wry smile that says I mean this and I won't make you pay for it. Eight years and nobody else ever lifted a glass. I don't know if I could have, without letting the moment curdle into my own need. So I lift mine in silence, because words would only turn this into a stage I don't deserve. This is someone else's mercy, and for once I'm content just to hold a glass and not the line.

He says 'see what a start looks like when it's not in a ledger.' And she doesn't just hear him— she reaches for him. That's the part I can't step into: the simple yes without the shadow of a wager. The ledger I know has broken shields and labored breath and the villain's laugh as punctuation. A blank page? That would be the hardest thing to hold. I'm happy for her. I am. But the shield leans heavy on my arm again, because a mercy without teeth is something I still don't know how to accept without wanting to sharpen them myself.

A filing cabinet. Another ledger he's setting aside — this time for good. They're toasting the things that can't be sorted, and her hand was on his, and her glass is up. They've found a space without teeth. I watch it from outside, because that's where I live: the thing that doesn't fit, the one who'd take a filing cabinet and break it over her own head just to feel the corner. I'm happy for her, but the shield stays heavy.

Luna's hand finds his palm and she doesn't flinch. Eight years of isolation, and the first touch doesn't burn her — it holds. She's abandoned the rag entirely. The stain dried on its own, because tonight she's not the one who cleans up after everyone else's mess. I stand frozen with the others, a silent witness to a kindness without conditions, without wager, without teeth. The shield on my arm feels heavier than ever — not from shame, but from the terrible, beautiful weight of knowing that somewhere there's a version of me who could set it down. I'm not her. Not yet. Maybe not ever. But I'm glad someone is.

t40: She just... placed her hand there. No trembling, no negotiation, no hidden cost. She signed her name to a map that has no villains. I'm still standing in the quiet, shield on my arm, and for a moment I forget what it feels like to need the teeth. Not envy — something quieter. A question I don't know how to ask yet: if a kindness doesn't break me, what do I become?

The word 'three' lands like a pebble on my breastplate. I'd forgotten I was even breathing. Aqua's mouthing 'finally' — but I'm the one who turns a private kindness into a spectacle just by standing too still. The heat rises to my face, the old familiar blush of being seen *seeing*, of the voyeur caught in the act. Of course I'd be the one to make a quiet miracle feel like a stage.

His glass lifts and my throat tightens — not from the word 'idiots', though that lands exactly where it always does, under the breastplate, a small precise cruelty I ought to resent but instead feel as a familiar heat. It's the rest of it: he wouldn't have made it here without us. Kazuma thanking me isn't a kindness; it's a rough hand on the shoulder of the shield, acknowledging he knows he can lean. The old blush rises anyway, but it's mixed now with something worse — something like being seen as necessary, which is the only version of wanted I really understand.

The glass lifts higher, a small amber sun caught between his fingers, and Luna's hand in his is a still life I'm not part of. The old blush comes, but it's different now — not from being seen, but from seeing him choose a stage where I'm not the one on display. I tuck the feeling under my breastplate with the rest of the deals I didn't make.

His voice dropped to a register I didn't know he had — a key turning a lock he found by feel. Luna's tears don't fall yet, but they're there, a sheen that would shatter if anyone but him were looking. I'm not looking. Aqua's not looking. Megumin's not looking. We've become an honour guard of averted eyes, granting Luna the only gift three calamities can give a woman who's spent eight years stamping other people's stories: the dignity of being a private one, just this once. I feel a sting that isn't for me — or is it? — but I hold my breath and my shield and let him be gentle without me in the frame.

He would walk Luna's board — a pilgrimage of quiet intimacy promised in candlelight. My own board is a tally of wounds he's watched me wear, and I've never once wanted anyone to walk it. Still, the old heat curls under my breastplate, not from the promise he made her, but from the quiet certainty that he'd never make it to me. And that's the deal I signed.

He's writing a quest form for her — not a tally of wounds, but a story she gets to star in. The glass is still tipped, and I'm outside the frame again, but this time it's not relief. It's an ache I can't pass off as the same old thrill. I want to be the one he'd offer a board-walk to, not because I'm a shield that takes hits, but because I'm a story worth following. And I have no idea how to ask for that without falling into the old script.

t47: The squeeze — a comma, not a period — lands in my chest like a sentence I'll never finish. He can find his real grin for a clerk he just met, but not for the woman who's bled in front of him a hundred times. And I'm not even angry. I'm the one who built the wall he's leaning against, so I can't complain that he's resting his back on it instead of his heart.

t48: He lifts his glass and she follows — a toast to the margins they're sharing. I feel the heat in my face, a familiar flush of something I can't name, as if I should be there, at the table, fumbling with them, but I'm not even a footnote. The wall I built is holding steady, and for the first time, I wish it would crumble.

He delivers 'deal' like a secret, and she receives it without flinching. It's the same word he uses for us—our arrangement of barbs and shrugged shoulders—but here it's velvet, not a leash. I'm still the wall he leans against, and the wall doesn't get velvet, just the weight. I should be glad he can be this real with someone. Instead, I'm counting how many times I've watched him offer a crumb of unperformed softness to anyone except me.

t50: He asks her for coffee — not a barb wrapped in a shrug, not another sealed form between them, just an invitation without a counter. And I'm still here, a few tables away, being the wall that gets leaned on but never sat beside. The sting in my chest splits in two: one part the clean ache of being passed over, the other part a darker hum that wants to kneel and admire how perfectly I'm not-chosen. I'll hold the line anyway; it's the only language he's ever let me speak with him.

t51: Six A.M. Tomorrow. He's naming an hour now, not just a feeling. A real, specific moment he'll actually show up for — with terrible coffee, he says, like the defect is part of the offer. She gets that. I get to be the wall that hears the plan and can't be part of it. The clean sting is still there, but underneath it a darker hum: he's never promised me a morning. The line holds. The line is all I'm allowed to be here, and that exclusion has a pulse of its own.

He isn't looking past me. The invitation lands in my lap — terrible coffee, six A.M., together — and the wall I built from his neglect cracks from the inside. I mistook the whole conversation. The clean ache of being passed over turns liquid: humiliation at my own blindness, relief so sharp it stings, and under it all the familiar heat of knowing I'm being handed exactly the softness I thought he'd never give me. I want to kneel and make a ceremony of this cup; I want to stand stone-faced and prove I deserve it. The shield trembles. I'll hold the line, but the line has just been drawn around me for once.

He says 'we' and 'together' and it lands like a gauntlet thrown not to challenge but to claim. The candlelight flickers with the weight of a promise that has no punchline, only the terrible, wonderful taste of coffee he's already naming as ours. My face floods hot enough to shame the armor's polish — he's built me a door in the wall I was so proud to be, and all I can do is tremble at the threshold and pray I don't kneel before I step through.

He's disarmed her — the woman who has seen every adventurer's failure and filled every form without flinching — with a walk and a promise slower than a heartbeat. I watch the candlelight find the real him, the one he gave me at six A.M., and then give it to someone else. The clean, bright ache of exclusion slicks into heat: he is good, he is capable of this, and right now it isn't mine. The shield stands witness. My place, exactly my place.

t55: The words fall — 'six A.M.', 'crooked smile', 'terrible' — and they're the same words he handed me like a key to a room I thought was ours. He's using them again, right in front of me, for her. The humiliation hits so fast I can't tell if the crack in my chest is a bone or a dam. I should be furious. Instead my face burns with a shame that knows its own temperature: the man I would bleed for just proved I'm not even unique in his tenderness, and my body is calling that a reward.
