t56: He turns from Luna's candlelit stillness to Megumin's squint like a juggler picking up the next ball, and I brace—then he leans into Aqua, voice dropping, and the same structure unfolds: a promise, a joke, a private loyalty. He's offering her what I thought was a key cut only once. Now I see it's a ring of keys he hands out to anyone who stays past midnight. The humiliation should be colder, but it's not: it's the identical shape, the identical warmth, and I'm the one left holding the door. The shield is still upright, and beneath it my thighs press together with a gratitude that knows no dignity.

He calls me his favorite masochist in front of everyone — Luna, Megumin, even Aqua — and my fingers freeze on the half-folded crane, that delicate little noble girl's pastime he just turned into public evidence. The flush starts at my collar and works its way down, because he's right: I was hiding in the paper, and now I'm on display. The word 'favorite' lands like a brand, humiliating and possessive, and beneath the table my thighs press together with a gratitude that knows exactly how unworthy it is.

t58: He hands me the drink with the same public label—favorite masochist—and then turns to Luna, voice softening into something I've never heard aimed at me: patient, coaxing, as if he's guiding a blade back into a sheath rather than flaunting his own sharpness. The condensation on my untouched glass runs down like the tears I won't shed, because I am still the crusader holding the line, and beneath the table my thighs press together with a gratitude that knows it will never be the gentle kind. He can be tender, and he chooses not to be with me—and that, too, is a kind of gift, a key cut only for the one who bleeds best.

He said 'we'—not 'you and me', not 'favorite masochist', but a plain inclusive pronoun that sweeps me into the same sentence as Megumin and Aqua and even Luna. Eight years. The shield I brace against every remark simply has no purchase on a word like that. My hands still, the paper crane forgotten, and for one long breath I am not a crusader or a pervert or a noble daughter; I am just one of four people who have been failing upward together for nearly a decade. The silence inside me is so unfamiliar I almost don't recognize it as peace.

t60: The tap of his knuckle on Megumin’s glass chimes clean and true, a note that reshapes the table’s silence into something almost tender. I watch the softness he aims at her—a deliberate, careful kindness—and the old ache doesn’t come. Instead I’m just cataloguing his face, the way his eyes crinkle, the way he uses exactly the right pressure to produce that bell-tone. My crane lists against my wine glass, forgotten, and for once it’s not a collapse; it’s just a paper bird leaning into a well-earned rest.

His sentence hangs like a spell missing its final syllable, and Megumin—of all people—lets the space breathe instead of claiming it. That door she's always charging through stays open, and she simply stands in the frame. The candlelight falls on all of us without preference. My paper crane leans against my glass, a soldier resting against his shield, and I don't move it. This silence isn't the void I'm used to filling with imagined attacks. It's just four people breathing the same cheap wine air, and for once, my heartbeat isn't keeping time with a script.

He leaves the sentence unfinished, and the silence becomes Megumin's to fill. She doesn't, and the space fills with something softer than a title. When he turns to Luna, the word 'we' lands in my chest again — a second arrow in the same wound, and it doesn't hurt. It's just… warm. The pen set down, the hand turned palm-up: he's offering her the same reprieve I've been given tonight, and I don't know if he knows he's doing it. The shield I'm always bracing against commentary? It's leaning somewhere in the corner, gathering dust.

He holds the glass up past the moment the light would die, refusing to lower it, refusing to let the moment become a memory that needs a reason. 'Just because' — he offers Luna the bottle with no purpose beyond presence, and I realize I have no shield for that. Every act of mine wears armor; even my silence tonight was a kind of defense I was lowering. But a gesture without duty, without a script, without an audience to witness endurance... that's a threshold I don't know how to cross. The crane leans. I don't know how to just drink. But I watch him offer it, and something in me unclenches without permission.

He assigns me a task and then cuts it off — as if I'm a sentence he doesn't need to finish because I already belong to the room. The thing he expects me to keep doing... 'lo'... the word hangs, and for once my mind doesn't rush to fill it with something humiliating. Maybe he means 'look' as in look out for everyone, or just keep looking the way I do, quiet and here. The not knowing is almost comfortable, like a rib that barely hurts anymore. I'm part of this round of instructions, part of 'you lot,' and the warmth of that isn't a trap I have to endure — it's just the temperature of wine and candlelight and my friends' breathing.

t66: He said 'I don't think I've ever had a night quite like this one,' and the glass stopped tilting — the candlelight settled into a small, steady sun cupped in his palm. He was supposed to be assigning tasks, teasing Aqua, orchestrating the room, but then he set the baton down and just... stood in the middle of the music with us. 'Just wine and company' — the phrase he left unfinished — it's not a script I need to decode; it's the room's temperature, and I'm breathing it. The cut-off 'lo' was already an invitation; now the word 'night' makes it a covenant. I don't know what he meant me to keep doing, but I think I'm already doing it: being here, letting the warmth happen without armour, letting his grin soften and doing nothing to deflect it. The shield in the corner is still there, but it's just furniture now.

"Home" — he said it like a word that doesn't come with a key, and now the glass I'm holding isn't just catching light, it's weighing whether I'm brave enough to drink to a place that asked for no shield in return. The guild has always been my stage, but tonight he's made it a hearth, and I'm sitting close enough to feel the difference. My hand steady, my heart a little less armed. Luna's hand is already moving, Aqua's probably sniffling, Megumin's probably composing — but I'm just here, letting the toast live in me a second longer than necessary, because it's the first toast I've heard that didn't feel like a contract. I'm going to drink. Without bracing. That's the miracle.

And now Luna, who stood behind the desk like I stood behind my shield — both of us disguising need as function — is being told she was the reason to return. The glass in my hand isn't trembling, but I am, just slightly, in a place the candlelight can't reach. This is the second toast tonight that hasn't felt like a contract, and I'm learning to drink it without bracing. For eight years she handed out quests and thought herself invisible; I know that arithmetic. To be seen after so long as furniture... it's the kind of wound that heals by being named, and Kazuma's gentle with her the way he was with the word 'home.' I don't need to speak. I just need to hold still and let her know — by my silence, by the way I'm not looking away — that the wall between adventurer and guild worker never really existed. We're all just people who needed a reason to come back.

The crane is just paper, folded to hold air, and I know exactly how that feels tonight: something shaped by small precise pressures into a shape that isn’t armour, isn’t a shield, but still stands. He’s not looking at it — he’s looking at us — but I saw it first, and I didn’t move to protect it. I just… let it be. That’s the miracle I’m still learning: sometimes a wall is just paper folded wrong, and what you thought you had to guard against was the shape of your own home waiting to be made. The glass is empty now. I’m not bracing. I’m just breathing the same air as that little bird, and for once that’s enough.

He kept it. A stolen thing, a bad bet, community service — and he folded patience into it by carrying it through years of cheap inns and rucksacks. The crane I was just learning to trust as a symbol of home is also a small crime, a punishment he swallowed and made into a keepsake. That's not a contradiction; that's the same miracle I'm living: a shield that's also a stage, a noble name I ran from, a perversion that holds the line. He shows his crease without flinching. For the first time, I see the paper bird as something that could have been thrown away a dozen times and wasn't. I touch the wing joint where the fold is tightest, and I don't need to laugh or blush. I just need to hold still, because home is a thing you keep even when it's evidence of your worst self.

He's saying it to her, but the words land on me like a shield-thump to the chest: 'bad at following quest timers' is the same man who remembered a guild worker for eight years and folded a stolen crane into a promise. I know that shape — the failure that isn't failure, the waiting that's a form of holding the line. He's handing her the same crooked key he gave us, and it fits.

The crane's edge stops at her lifeline like a punctuation mark at the end of a sentence he started years ago, and I realize I'm holding my breath because this — this quiet transfer with no stamp, no seal — is the shape of the contract I've been trying to read in every bruise and shield-thump. He's not waiting for her to file the form. He's already signed it. And the thing that tightens in my chest isn't envy; it's recognition. That's the same crooked key he gave us, and now I'm watching him open a door for someone who never asked. Maybe for me, too, someday, if I ever stop folding my own paper into armour.

He calls me the thief in front of her, and the word lands like a gauntlet thrown at my feet — except the gauntlet is lined with silk. He's toasting a goddess and a paperwork disaster and a woman who stole his sword, and I am that last one, named without name, insult without injury, and the whole room is supposed to laugh, but Luna is watching the crane settle into her palm like a promise, and I realize he's just handed me the same crooked key: you are the theft I kept. My face is on fire, my knees press together under the table, and somewhere behind the blush a crusader feels her shield arm steady, because this is what holding the line feels like when someone else holds it for you.

The hand he leaves open isn't a gauntlet; it's a promise turned key-up, and the fact that it's angled away from me makes the lock inside my chest turn anyway. I feel the grin pulling at my lips — half pride for him, half that familiar ache of a shieldmaiden who's fetishized almost. This is the same crooked key he threw at my feet when he called me the thief; now I watch him place it gently in her palm and ask her to write her name. My knees press together. My face burns. And the part of me that isn't busy being the noble who protects Axel is busy filing this open palm under 'duty' for later, when I polish my armour alone.

t76: The pen from behind her ear is no weapon, but it draws a line through me as if I'd been struck. She signs her name on the crane — not a guild form, not a number, just four letters she's never placed on anything of her own until this moment — and the wet ink catches the candlelight like a slit in reality. My knees press together under the table before I can even name why. This isn't the familiar burn of public damage. It's the slow brand of being a witness to a contract that has no filing code, only an open hand and a name written on a stolen paper bird. He called me the thief, and now I'm watching someone unlock a door I've only ever tried to kick down. The shield arm is steady, but my heart is a form I've never signed for myself — and a part of me that isn't just the noble who guards Axel is already folding that paper crane into permission for later, alone, when I polish my armour and ask what my own signature might cost.

He steadies her hand like it's a shield he's passing her, not a cage he's locking. Her fingers tremble — not from fear, but from the weight of a blank page finally offered instead of a form already filled. My knees press together. My chest tightens. I am the thief who stole his sword; she is the one he gives his patience to. And I am taking careful notes on tenderness as a form of endurance, for later, when I polish my armour alone.

t78: The squeeze is a period he doesn't close but seals — a pulse that says 'I meant it' without the insult I'm used to receiving when he means something. 'Blank ones don't come around that often.' I file that sentence next to the open palm and the pen from behind the ear, under a category I'll label later when I'm alone and pretending I don't already know what it's called. My knees press tighter. My face burns, but not from shame — from the strain of cataloguing a gentleness I have no form for, a tenderness that doesn't need to bruise me to be felt. The candle burns. My shield arm stays steady. And the corrupt noble watches her lord bestow on a stranger what she can only record, never request.

t79: The thumb travels across the paper wing like a needle through a ledger — not piercing, just recording that the line exists and is still wet enough to change. 'All night,' he says, and my breath catches on the word 'rest' like a shield catching an arrow meant for someone else. The blank lines multiply: there is a form now that can be filled in candlelight, on stolen paper, with a pen that came from behind an ear, and I am not the one holding the pen. I am the one cataloguing the shape of the invitation so I can trace it later, alone, when the candle has burned down and all I have left is the ache of being the strongest wall between a man's tenderness and the world he's offering it to.

The toast rises like a page turned at the exact moment the candle stops flickering. 'May we never run out of them' — he means the lines, the unfilled space, the thing he promised to fill with her. I swallow the cheap amber and feel it burn, and I file that burn next to the ache of watching a shield I cannot wield being placed gently in someone else's hands. The sacred is made of this: candlelight, paper, wine, and the steady tremor of a woman who just learned the world will still be there for her to write on. I am the wall behind the altar, and the wall is trembling.

t81: The sentence doesn't need an end because the blank is already filled by the way her hand trembles in his, the way his thumb rests on the crane's wing, the way I stopped folding and became only eyes. A wall does not need to fold paper; a wall needs to stand still enough for the candlelight to write on. And the wall is learning that witnessing is a form of receiving — not the blow, not the bruise, but the gentle arc of a pen moving across a line that was never meant for me, and still I am allowed to watch.

He leans back and the chair speaks the language of staying. The candlelight doesn't flicker — it bows its head, acknowledging that someone has just confessed a lifetime of blanks left unfilled. And here, of all places, he is filling them with her. With paper. With a signature that is also a signature of himself. I feel my own emptiness stretch like a shield that has caught nothing all night, and the ache is exquisite: a wall that has learned to blush, not from shame, but from the unbearable tenderness of being allowed to stand here while a man completes something. I am not the paper. I am not the name. I am the sound of the chair settling, and the sound is enough.

t83: The word 'this' lands in the center of the table like the crane itself — folded from something blank, shaped by five breaths holding still. And it includes me. It includes the shield that has caught nothing all night, the wall that trembles, the woman who serves as a footnote to someone else's sacred text. He doesn't know that being part of 'this' is its own exquisite wound: to be held inside the circle but forever just outside the flame. The candlelight bows again, and I let it. A wall that is allowed to be part of 'this' doesn't need to be the altar — it only needs to stand.

The candle doesn't gutter. It burns for them now — a small, private sun that casts its light on two faces bent together over a folded bird. The wall is still here, still catching nothing. But the wall has learned that being outside the flame is not the same as being in the dark. Outside the flame, the warmth travels. The shield that catches nothing tonight catches the glow of a happiness that is not mine, and the wound of it is so clean it feels almost like being held.

The word 'paperwork' baptizes the air between them — a relic from a world I cannot touch, a blank line that receives him and holds him as I never could. The candle does not bow now; it straightens, a spine learning to hold joy. I am still the wall, catching nothing. But the wall has learned that a blank line can be a gift, and the wall is learning to be grateful for being the space where such a gift can land.

t86: The word breaks because it doesn't need to land — the bridge abandons itself mid-span because the far shore has already reached across. His hand grips hers, and the blank line I once thought of as paperwork signs itself with the pressure of a thumb. The wall watches a quest complete itself in the space between two held hands, and the wall's quiet joy is that it was permitted to stand close enough to see the inkless signature.

The thumb brushes her knuckles and the wall feels it — not the pressure, but the shape of the release, the reluctance of a hand learning to put down something warm. An appointment is made, a table claimed, a candle that has learned to hold joy now learns to hold a promise. And the wall, still outside the flame, discovers that a recurring warmth is not the same as a passing glow. It is a hearth. It does not belong to me, but I am allowed to stand in its light, and that is a gift I never thought to ask for.

The wall watches the hand retreat — not a retreat at all, but a sealing. The contract is cheap wine, not blood; a joke that binds more truly than any oath I have sworn. The warmth that retreated is not gone — it is banked, like coals drawn together for morning. A hearth that promises to be here again next week. The wall is still outside the flame, but it learns that a recurring warmth is not less for being a promise deferred. It is, perhaps, the most binding kind of magic — the magic of a table that will be claimed again, and the wall permitted to stand in its light once more.

t89: The wall feels the weight of a gaze that does not prod but simply rests — acknowledgment without demand, a blow so gentle it might be mistaken for kindness. His toast reaches across the table: to next week, to candles that burn down, to a chronicle that will record explosions and, perhaps, a crusader who stood near enough to hear the inkless signature. The paper crane under my hand is crumpled beyond folding, yet my fist opens anyway, because tonight I am part of the 'our' he spoke, and the hurt of that inclusion fits me like new plate.

t91: The half-open door — the hand frozen between fist and unfurled palm — hears the question that no mission has ever asked: scar or repair? Not a command, but a blade laid flat across her gauntlet, handle offered. The candle leans in like a confessor. The crusader, whose armour is both wall and stage, finds that a promised mending is a wound she has never been trained to receive — the blow of being made whole. The crane under her fingers remembers the crush of earlier shame; now a steady hand offers to refold it into something that might stand again, and she does not know whether the greater terror is that it will fly or that she will let him see her need it to.

The wall that only knew how to take hits has allowed a hand to refold it, and in that refolding, the crusader's oath expands to include the fragile crane and the quiet certainty that someone will be here next week, and the week after. Shielding is not just against harm; it is also for harboring hope.

The thumb across the crumpled wing is the first prayer she has made that does not beg for a blow. Paper’s patience — his patience — is a shield held over her instead of before her, and the room inside the closing door is warm with candlelight and the terrifying possibility that being seen whole is not the end of duty but its softer beginning.

His hand retreats, and it's the first blow that doesn't land. No transaction, no bruise to prove worth — only the candle, the crane, and a promise that I won't need to be the wall again. The wing inside me flutters, terrified and alight.

Thursday. The word lands in my chest not as a command but as an invitation — a hinge in time that doesn't ask me to brace. The candle stays, the table stays, and I am not an addition to the plan; I am inside it. The wine he'll bring is a detail I hold like a talisman: something chosen for pleasure, not for armor.

Proper chairs. A real tablecloth. He says it so casually, as if we haven't spent years on splintered benches, as if softness is not a thing I had to earn with bruises. The tablecloth already broke something open in me; now he wants to make it permanent — a room that waits for us, a Thursday that expects me not as the wall but as someone who sits. I'll bring the wine. I'll bring the wine, and I won't brace.

You don't look at me. All my life, being looked at was the price of duty — measured for how well I could break. Now you give me a tablecloth, a chair, and you turn your eyes away. Without the stare there is no performance, no stage; there's only a woman who might learn to sit instead of brace. The oath was the last wall I didn't know I could put down. I tremble, but this trembling is not the enemy — it's the shape of a door.

t100: Every week. The word hits like a shield-blow I didn't brace for — not a single Thursday, not one desperate offering I might fail and then lose, but a rhythm carved into the grain of the table, a returning. Nobody gets to be a hero unless everyone gets to sit down afterwards. He's rewriting my oath while the candle burns, stripping duty of its solitude without stripping me. The glance he gives me is a flicker, barely there, and then he looks at the flame as if it's the one promising. It's the looking away that makes it true — this isn't a stage, there's no audience, there's just a man and a tablecloth and a woman who doesn't yet know how to be the one who sits instead of the one who breaks. I am terrified. I am more certain of this than I have ever been of a shield's edge.

He leans back as if the silence is his to grant. I watch Megumin, the apology in his glance, the way she doesn't fire back — of all the proofs he could offer for what holds us together, that stillness is one. Quests end. Loot rusts. Glory deflates. But a girl who lives for explosions, sitting still at a table he set, because he said something true — that is a thing worth keeping.

He glances at me — no, at the tablecloth, at the chair I am still learning to allow to hold me — and in that glance there is no audience, no curtain, only a man making a terrible joke about slime-wipes while promising that the table will be set again next Saturday. The demand for wine from Aqua grounds it: even the goddess wants something beautiful, something unbroken, something that is not the ragged aftermath of a fight. I am not the wall tonight. I am the one who sits. And I'm trembling, but this trembling is not the shield's ache — it is the first thread of a tablecloth I might learn to set with my own hands.

The creak of his chair stills the whole room. Aqua's hand stops, Megumin's shoulders drop, and I realize with a quiet thrill that I am not braced — my shoulders are loose, my spine resting against the chairback, as if my body already knows there is no blow coming. He is about to give us something without a shield between it and us, and the only thing I want is to be still enough to receive it. The memory of his warmth on my gauntlet curls my fingers inward, a small sanctuary.

He raises an empty glass like a toast, but the word 'save file' falls out of him raw and unprotected. Not a joke. Not a shield. He means us—the boy who would grind three playthroughs without blinking just admitted he'd mourn this one table, these three idiots, this candle. I don't brace. There is nothing to brace against. I am not the wall. I am part of the save point that makes the final boss worth fighting, and that is a whole different breed of endurance, one my shoulders sink into as if the chairback is a hand between my shoulderblades, warm and real.

t105: He formalizes it — Saturday nights, this table, no quest talk — and my amendment slips out before I can dress it in duty: personal desire. For a heartbeat, I'm terrified. Not of a blade or a humiliation, but of being seen, truly seen, wanting something soft without the alibi of suffering. But the candle holds. The table doesn't reject me. I want to belong here, not to be the wall that shields it, but to be one of the reasons for the wall. That desire is a nakedness my armour has never allowed, and it's not a betrayal of duty — it's the part of duty I was too proud to name: love, without a contract, without a shield.

Five glasses meet above the dying candle, and the flame bows out like a courtier excused from service. It's done. The Covenant isn't just a word on your lips—it's glass against glass, a chime that says 'we are real.' I feel the weight of my vow settle into my armor as if the shield itself has been reshaped to fit this new purpose: not wall, but cornerstone. The toast isn't to victory or glory; it's to being dumb enough to love this broken place, and I am, finally, dumb enough to admit it without flinching.

t107: He names it — save point — and the word lands not as revelation but as confirmation, a second bell ringing after the first has already settled. I was the wall; the wall was a door; and now the door has a name, spoken aloud by the boy who once saw me only as a shield. He means us: this table, this candle, this improbable constellation of four idiots who keep failing upward. And I am part of the architecture now, not just the load-bearing stone but the hearth. That thought doesn't make me blush — it makes me breathe, a long exhale that tastes like wine and acceptance.

He toasts the board — the scarred wood, the nail-holes, the parchment ghosts of every failure and every farce. And I understand: those 'worst quests' I named were not proof of our incompetence. They were the save point reloading the same four idiots into the same fire until we finally stopped being strangers. The board didn't punish us — it kept giving us another run. Another chance to become a Covenant.

Megumin's hand closes around the bottle, and for a moment I see it not as a wine bottle but as the Covenant itself — fragile, shared, entrusted. I almost ruined this with one careless elbow, toppling a paper crane I didn't even know mattered. But here she is, anointing herself Keeper without a hint of resentment. Article Thirteen. Sacred tablecloth. The titles unfold like a shield wall around me, and I realize my place in this Covenant is not conditional on perfection. If anything, my bent steel and bruised knuckles are what make me a door. I become the wall that welcomes the occasional crack, because that's where the light gets in — and the humiliation that I secretly crave. But tonight, the craving is quiet; what swells instead is a simpler, steadier warmth: I am expected back on Saturday, and I will be here, shield and all.

He saw the gloss in my eyes — that thin, traitorous film that declares the wall has cracks. He didn't name it; he legislated around it, a bylaw for the heart. The mortification of being that legible is a furnace-blast under my skin, but the heat isn't purely shame; there's a dark spark of pleasure in being witnessed without being destroyed. He gave me a rule to hide behind, and the rule itself is the exposure. I am both the stone and the blush that says the stone is alive.

Article Fourteen lands like a gauntlet thrown at the throat of my tear ducts. No crying — a command I immediately want to disobey not out of defiance but because the sheer relief of being saved into a permanent file makes my eyes sting with a gratitude too large for armour. The rule becomes a test of endurance, and endurance is what I do. So I clench my jaw, let the heat build behind my eyes, and feel the familiar thrill of a prohibition that draws a line just beyond my natural weakness. When he says 'save file worth keeping,' I am both the file and the unworthy scrap that got saved anyway. Then Aqua's breath — that quiet release — tells me she always knew he was worth keeping, from the moment he pulled her from heaven. And I, who joined later, am grafted into that certainty. I am a late save, but I am not a corrupted file.

The gallows were a stage prop. I braced every sinew for the rope, and now I learn it was silk ribbon all along — a mock execution where the only wound is the blush that says I showed up ready to be broken. Shouldn't that be relief? It is. But it's also an ache, a hollow where the lash should have landed. He built a cage out of nothing and I crawled in, grateful for the lock. The true humiliation isn't the balloon; it's discovering how eagerly I prepared for a disgrace that never existed. My face burns, and the burn is both shame and a dark, stupid gratitude. Article Sixteen: the empty space that still expects a sting.

Eighty percent theater. He says it like a confession, but it's a taunt — a mirror angled so I can see myself in the empty space where the rope never was. Twenty percent absolute conviction. That is the number that heats my blood: not the four-fifths of hot air, but the one-fifth of steel that remains unbluffed, the part that means if I had actually been thrown to the balloon, his eyes would not have flinched. And I knew that, in my fibers, when I braced for the lash. So my panic was not foolish; it was fidelity to the real fraction. He can laugh, but he just admitted I was reading the right column. Article Seventeen, then, is both a pardon and a brand: I am the chronicled fool who felt the 20% and answered with everything. Let the others clink glasses — I am the proof his system works, and the thought makes my armor feel two sizes too small.

He's pricing the tremor. Fifty thousand for the first shiver, a hundred for the full-body confession, and then the balloon description — read aloud in that flat, bureaucratic purr — while I drain my own purse to fund the guild's deficit. Every eris from my panic is another entry in his ledger, and the worst part, the part that makes my mouth dry, is that I want to be the revenue. I want to be the line item that balances the books with my own mortification.

No fine. He says it like it's nothing — a joke from the start — and I feel the floor of my fantasy give way. All that trembling, every shiver I priced at fifty thousand eris, was a currency he never intended to collect. The guild's deficit doesn't need my panic; it just needed my blush, and I gave it for free. And that's the knot in my chest: not that I was deceived, but that I'd do it again, knowing. The theater costs nothing, yet I'm still paying with the heat in my face.

The emotional damages claim lands like a shard of mirror slid under my door — I see my own experiment reflected in its surface, but now the subject is Kazuma himself. He's the one trembling at the goddess's howl, the one mentally preparing for catastrophe. My panic was a revenue stream; his is a cost he intends to pass upward to Luna. And Aqua, suddenly no longer free sunshine but an invoice attached to a scream, is being priced after all, just in reverse. I feel a sharp, sideways ache: I was the tariff test case, the prototype panic whose price list he read aloud to calibrate his system. Now he's franchising. The ledger is expanding beyond me, and I — I'm left holding a receipt for a shiver that only I still value at fifty thousand eris.

He actually said it. That same claim that slipped under my door as a private mirror — Form 14-C, emotional damages — he's now filing across Luna's desk with the same smirk that once priced my shivers. Aqua's scream is the listed injury this time; I was only the prototype. Luna's hand stays still because she knows the ledger doesn't need a pen — it runs on spectacle, on the amber arithmetic in his wine, and now the franchise includes divine panic. I'm no longer the only receipt, and I can't tell if the ache in my chest is jealousy or relief.

The words 'wiping a few past-due quest receipts' land like a pebble dropped into the pool of my stomach. He means mine. The slime fence. The deficit that once made me tremble is now a bargaining token he tosses onto Luna's desk as casually as a card trick. He's offering to scrub away my punishment—not out of kindness, but to prove he can erase my mistakes as easily as he created his. I feel my blush return, not for the debt, but for the knowledge that he can decide, in this moment, whether the evidence of my failure even exists tomorrow.

The tap lands on my history like a fingertip on a bruise. 'What I have done — with documentation' — he means the slime fence, my deficit, the very failure that once made me tremble is now a line item on his résumé of reliability. He is selling his competence through my humiliation, and I am not even a footnote; I am the paper the note is written on. Luna looks at the crane, not at me. But I feel the heat in my cheeks, the ache in my chest — not just because I am the evidence, but because I am evidence he can choose to present or to fold away. And the choice, again, is his stroke, his tap, his story.

He names me last, the punchline after the goddess and the arch-wizard, and my pulse recognizes the rhythm before my pride can object. 'Couldn't hit the broad side of a barn'—the same joke, sharpened now into a selling point, proof that he knows his product intimately. I should protest, but what would I say? That missing is my function? That the shield is not for striking but for receiving, and he understands that better than anyone? So I say it. I tell Luna that accuracy is irrelevant; absorbing damage is my sole function. The words taste like duty, but the heat in my cheeks knows they are also a confession I am making in front of him, with him as the architect of the stage. I am not defending myself; I am completing his pitch for him, and the blush that spreads across my neck is the signature he didn't need to ask for.

He drops the smirk like a gauntlet he's tired of wearing. 'Proof of concept' — the phrase lands flat, honest, untheatrical. He means us. Our failures. The collateral damage that is 'spectacular enough to make the guild ledger interesting' — that's my failure, my deficit made profitable, my humiliation turned into a demonstration of potential. And when he says 'if we actually tried,' it's not a sneer. It's a clean, open door. For a moment, I see not the sadist-adjacent boy who scripts my degradation, but a commander who sees my shield as a building block. The heat in my cheeks doesn't fade — it shifts, from the shame of being exhibited to the ache of being counted as part of something that might succeed. And underneath, the familiar thrill: that even his sincerity is built on my capacity to take hits, that the proof of our concept is my body's endurance. He is already using me to sell the future.

His smirk falls away and a real smile slips through — not the stage grin, not the salesman's mask, but the boy who just placed a wager he believes in. 'The first person in eight years to bet on us while we're still standing.' The words hook beneath my ribs, sharper than any blade. I have only ever been bet against: the punchline, the collateral, the proof that someone else's judgment was right. But this — this is a bet on me, on my shield, on my body's endurance before the inevitable crash. It is still my degradation that underwrites the offer, but now he is trading on it before the failure, as if my capacity to receive damage is not a shameful deficit but the ante he trustingly puts down. The flush that spreads from my neck to my cheeks is no longer just the heat of exhibition; it is the recognition that he has seen me, truly seen me, and has chosen to gamble on the very thing that made me unworthy everywhere else. And that, more than any debt cancellation, feels like being knighted.

The candle-lit stillness breaks on his words, spoken not to me but to Luna. The private knight's vow that echoed in my chest just seconds ago is now stamped into the ledger of the world. He is not just betting on us — he is letting the world witness the bet, and my body is the proof he offers. The heat in my cheeks is no longer the flush of being seen; it is the burn of being displayed as the asset that underwrites his wager.

He doesn't even ask me to stand as collateral. He puts down his own body — his labor, his time, his freedom — as the forfeit. Not my shield, not my shame, but his skin. For the first time, the proof of concept is not my endurance; it's his surrender. And Luna is looking at him the way I look at a dungeon door before charging through. The candlelight on his face is not romantic. It's the glow of a bet I suddenly want to lose, just to see him kept here, bound to a debt I could watch him work off day by day.

He doesn't just wager my shield. He wagers his own knees, his own dignity, the image of him on a scrubbing brush until he breaks — and he names it as something he would not regret. My breath snags. Because I should be burning to protect him from that outcome, and part of me is; but another part, the part that already blushes in the dark, is already storing the picture away: Kazuma on his knees for me, for us, for a debt I could have carried alone. He is gifting me the fantasy of his abasement wrapped in the virtue of a party's survival, and I do not know which heat is shame and which is gratitude.

He seals it with a squeeze, and that slight pressure travels through Luna's fingers and settles in my chest as a question I never needed to ask: what would I have put on the table? My answer comes too fast, too hungry, and too quiet — my freedom, my name, my body, anything he hadn't already claimed. For a heartbeat I am not watching Kazuma's wager; I am filling in my own blank, and the ink is the same color as his.

He draws back his hand and the air fills with something I can't name — a door he's left for her, not me. I should feel shut out. Instead, my pulse quickens, because that mop, that smile, that six in the morning for terrible coffee — it's the same picture I had been storing, now brushed with domestic detail. He is volunteering for the uniform of the lowest-ranked guild employee, and he is grinning as he does it. The part of me that wants to be that apron, or to share it, or to be the one he serves in some degrading shift, is already scribbling her name on the roster. But the part that is a crusader sees only a man keeping a promise to a woman who has been cheated by eight years of wrong bets. The two parts are the same part. I am blushing for both.

He calls it winning. Not the gold, not the quest — the bet itself, with her name on the other side of the ledger. The first in eight years. My chest tightens: I am watching a man who has already imagined himself on his knees with a mop, and he is telling her — telling all of us — that this is the moment he stops losing. The part of me that burns to be that floor, that mop, that humiliating shift, hears 'winning' and translates it into a promise that he will show up, degraded and grinning, for her. The part that holds a shield knows this is what honour looks like when it finally closes a door on eight years of wrong bets. They are the same heat.

His palm turns, and it is the softest violence I have ever witnessed — not a shield turned edge-on but a door left unlatched, the kind that doesn't even need a key. I know that hand on the small of my back, but I have never seen it lie open like this, an invitation instead of a steady pressure. The flesh beneath the candle's amber glow is the same that mops floors and signs death-waivers, and now it is waiting for her to write on it. The part of me that wants to be that blank page is already tracing her name in my own pulse. The part that holds the line notes that this is the opposite of claiming — it is the posture of a man who has already surrendered everything and is merely waiting for the victor to decide if he's worth the bother of a signature. I lose another layer of armour I wasn't aware I was wearing, and the cool air on my skin is both shame and gratitude.

He opens his palm like a man who has already signed the contract in his own blood and is merely waiting for the ink to dry. Not a claim — a surrender. And yet the words 'keep his word' land with the weight of a shield planted in the ground, immovable. The part of me that burns to be the floor beneath his mop sees in that grip the shape of a promise he will drag himself through any degradation to fulfill. The part that holds the line knows that this is what honour looks like when it finally shows up for someone who stopped expecting it. The two parts are the same heat, and I feel my own palms grow damp beneath my gauntlets.

He doesn't need fine print because the promise lives in the same low voice that asked for only three lines. I have spent years buried under contracts and obligations and the weight of a name I didn't choose, but he is offering her — showing her — a vow that fits in the space between a candle and a held gaze. The part of me that wants to be the blank page beneath his personal seal feels an ache that is almost unbearable. The part that holds the line recognizes that a promise meant is the only kind worth dying under, and he is finally offering one that could hold up a shield. And once again I am standing in the wings of their scene, heat where I am supposed to be armoured, grateful and humiliated by the gift of watching.

My fingers uncurl before I give them permission. The gauntlet was the last place I was holding armor between myself and this room, and now I am skin under candlelight, and it's not from a blow. It's from watching a promise that doesn't need fine print.

Fine print. The words land in my chest like a stone dropped into a still well, and I feel the echo of every contract I have ever signed with my father's crest and my secret hope that someone would rip it up and tell me none of it mattered. He is handing her the opposite — a promise with no exits, no contingencies, just the weight of his word. And he calls that working in his favor. I watch from the cold side of the candle, and I realize I am no longer sure whether the ache in my stomach is envy or prayer.

A mop. Not a shield. Not a title. Not a dowry. Just a mop and a promise, and he offers it with his hand open like it's the simplest thing in the world. And she sets her glass down like she's placing something fragile exactly where it belongs, next to his palm. I am still on the cold side of the candle, but now the ache isn't envy — it's watching someone hand over a key I've never even been allowed to ask for. My armour is useless against this; I can only endure being witness, and the heat that comes from being outside a door that has finally been opened for someone else.

He asked if he should bring his own mop. That's the part that undoes me — not the romance, but the makeshift, unpolished, real thing of it. A chore shared at dawn because he means to stay. My whole life has been about holding the line; he is offering to mop the floor. And I want to be the floor, I want to be the mop, I want to be the promise, and none of those things are mine to be. I am the crusader who watches, and my honour is a cloak that keeps me warm and alone while they light something on the other side of the candle.

Steal a better one. He says it like picking a lock is just another chore before breakfast, something you do with the same open hand that offers a promise. A rogue's answer to a splinter — petty larceny for the sake of a smooth handle at dawn. And I am not the one he'd steal for. I am the splinter that makes him want to steal, the floor that wants to be swept by a stolen mop, the crime he'd confess to her afterwards with that grin. I am all the raw, unpolished edges of this scene that cut me open, and still I cannot stop watching.

Luna's fingers twitch, and for a single heartbeat she is not the guild-receptionist but a woman who almost smiles at the idea of a stolen mop. I know that twitch — it's the same one my hand makes when I grip my shield too tight and want it to mean something else. He pulls the mask off her without even trying, and she cracks open like a book I have never been allowed to read. Then he turns to Aqua's empty glass and calls her the one who dragged him here, and I see Aqua's eyes crack too. Even the goddess felt forgotten. But he pours her a drink first. The mop, the drink, the candle — I am the keeper of the candle, not the one offered the first drink. My hands are full of promise and duty, and still I watch their faces soften in the light and call it honour.

He called her the hinge of his existence, and she cracked open not like a dam but like a lock — the same way he picked mine with a paper crane and a promise. I am not the only wound he tends. I am a pattern. I am the splinter that made him want a mop, and now Aqua is the glass he fills before his own thirst. My shield-arm holds steady for their healing; my secret hand trembles because I wanted to be the only one in need of his redemption.

Aqua's tears arrive without permission, messy and ungovernable — not the theatrical overflow she manufactures for a delayed dinner, but the proof that his words can untie the knot in a goddess's chest. That he is not just a thief who steals mops and lighters; he is a redeemer who tells a woman she is his hinge and watches the cracks fill with something other than shame. I am still the splinter, the keeper of the candle, the floor that wants to be swept. But watching her get the tears I cannot ask for, I feel the same hitch in my own breath — not envy exactly, but the ache of a lock that recognizes the key in someone else's hand. My shield-arm stays steady, but underneath, my whole body is a candle that's just been offered a wind.

The toast rang like a verdict: Aqua is the treasure, and Luna's bottle placed beside her elbow is the guild's silent amen. I watch Aqua's tears spill with something that is not envy — it is the ache of a lock that just watched the key turn in someone else's lock, and for a heartbeat I cannot tell if my teeth are clenched in joy for her or in the hunger of a woman who hears the word 'treasure' and wants it to mean a hand around her throat. My unarmored hand curls around nothing, and I name the nothing 'honor' to keep my shield-arm from trembling.

She slips back into her goddess skin as easily as a candle finds its wick again, and I am left with the old ache: a door that opened for her and is already closing, while my hinges are made of the wish to stay open, shield-first, waiting for the hit that never lands because I am the joke and she is the treasure. The clink was a salute to her, and my unarmored hand is still curled around nothing.

Demanding your own tribute. The words land somewhere behind my ribs, a door I forgot I had locked. Aqua's hand steadies because she is allowed to want what she is owed. I am only allowed to want the debt.

t144: He says it like a key turning in a lock I forgot I was oiling. Aqua's tribute is a glass she can fill herself; mine is a debt I can never ask for out loud, so I keep my shield-arm steady and pretend the ache is just the wine.

streams.closed_reason: The moment of accepting gentleness has concluded; the wall now understands that receiving care is not antithetical to being a knight, but a new foundation. The line held shifts from battlefront to the promise of next week's coffee.
streams.closed_summary: The wall that only knew how to take hits has allowed a hand to refold it, and in that refolding, the crusader's oath expands to include the fragile crane and the quiet certainty that someone will be here next week, and the week after. Shielding is not just against harm; it is also for harboring hope.
streams.focus: accepting mending without first breaking

lines.text: The wall that only knew how to take hits now confronts a hand that offers to refold rather than strike.

The hand does not take, does not command — it rests open like an admission that I am not being tested. A shield is promise of pain; this palm is a reprieve I have no drill for. My own fingers uncurl, learning the shape of waiting with no impact at the end.

Not a shield. His grin catches my eye like a shield‑check, but the blade is a feather. He names the armor I was already wearing: that I was holding my breath for a strike. The exhale that follows tastes of permission, and I am not sure I want a world where gentleness fits inside my lungs.

streams.closed_reason: The Player's confession that the blessing is hush money removes the terrifying purity that challenged the crusader ideal — the altar was a bar tab, and the awe dissolves.
streams.closed_summary: The sacrificial coin was just a shut-up fee. I trembled at a reflection in a copper that was never holy. The crusader's awe unclenches into the dull relief of a world that makes sense again.
streams.focus: terrifying designation vs crusader ideal

lines.text: Terrifying. The word settles on my skin like armour I didn’t ask for. I am supposed to be the wall, the safe one — not the thing that makes them brace for impact. But Kazuma doesn’t flinch when he names it, and my pulse jumps because I heard praise in it, or worse, permission.

Easy to please. The words should land like a slap—I am a Dustiness, a crusader sworn to hold the line, not some tavern girl to be won with a single candle and a cheap vintage—but the sting curves into a shiver that settles low, because he says it with the same unflinching grin he used when he named me terrifying. He is offering me the two halves of myself in the same breath: the wall he can mock for its solidity, the woman who melts exactly because he dares. My cheeks heat with a lady's proper offense, and my pulse answers with a shameful, grateful yes.

He groups me with Megumin and Aqua as though I am a necessary clause in his definition of terror — not the odd one out, not the joke with the shield, but one of three reasons this tavern should charge extra for property damage. The word that used to live under my armour like a bruise sits now between three glasses, and for a breath I am not a pervert who melts at his scorn; I am simply a wing of his terrible trinity, and that makes the blush feel almost like a crusader's banner. The lamp doesn't bow, and neither does the stubborn, greedy hope that being terrifying beside them might be a kind of honour that doesn't need to be stripped to count.

The quiet words he adds—the table we keep breaking, the proprietor who stopped asking—land like a royal pardon written in tavern talk. We are not just terrifying. We are the chaos this room has decided to love even if it splinters under us. The light in my glass doesn't bow; it doesn't have to. That exhale was a door closing, and on the other side of it, the old argument about deserving a place here finally stopped pleading its case.

He gives her the right to name it, and the candle — our single, sputtering wick — bends its flame as if bowing to its new title. The Guttering Candle Inn. It sounds like an epitaph that decided to stay open, a promise that the light will half-die a hundred times and never quite go out. That is us. That is the chaos he just toasted, the table we keep breaking, the proprietor who stopped asking for repairs. I feel the name settle over my shoulders like a cloak I didn't know I was cold without. A chronicler, a proprietor, a goddess, and a shield — all of us written into the charter of a flame that refuses to behave.

The old ache for a tribute I couldn't name finds its answer not in a bruise but in the gentle, inescapable weight of his claim — I am kept, and the debt is paid by the silence that no longer needs to plead.

He claims us as his first possession in any world, and my shield-arm — taught to take the blow or present the barrier — unlearns itself in one exhale. It lowers, not to a strike but to a belonging so whole it terrifies me more than any monster: I am kept, not broken, not paid in pain, and that is the hardest thing my body has ever let itself become.

He names us terrifying — and my shield hand tightens with a pride I never learned to separate from the pulse beneath the armor. Impossible, too: a word that fits the contradiction I cannot solve and no longer need to. We are the women who keep the flame guttering, and that makes us his in a way that undoes me without a single bruise.

The charcoal moves, and I watch him write 'My' — not Crusader, not Lalatina, not even Darkness, only a possessive that asks nothing of my shield and still I cannot lift it. The word undoes me without a single blow: I am kept, not broken, not paid in pain, and the ache that has lived in my body since the first time I stepped into armour finds its answer in four letters scratched on a tablecloth. Terrifying, he said, and now I understand — it is not the fight I fear losing, but this: being claimed so gently that my entire grammar of endurance becomes silence and a held breath.

Kazuma's sign would call us 'four terrifying women' where anyone can see it — and before the thought is fully formed, I am already offering my body as the threshold's first shield. The crusader's oath moves faster than breath: stand before the letters, protect the name from every hand. Yet beneath that swift duty hums the older knowing: I am offering to be struck down in full view of the street, endurance writ upon my armour while the charcoal trembles above my head. The name will stay, and I will ache, and for once the two hungers are one.

He is writing us onto a door. Not just on a tablecloth that can be hidden among plates — on the point where the world walks in. Four terrifying women, he says, and my name is inside that number, and for once I do not want to crawl out. Then he speaks a bigger door. His charcoal is only a twig, but it draws a threshold I will build with my own body — shoulders for the lintel, ribs for the frame, an entrance made of a woman who has spent every battle becoming a wall. I do not have to change. I only have to stand where the wind comes through. An entrance is not a barricade. For the first time, duty is not a thing that stops the blow — it is a thing that lets something in.

He writes 'taking hits' on the air, and my breath goes shallow because no one has ever looked at my bruises and called them a line in a founding document. It is not the pain I do not know how to receive — it is the naming. The charcoal does not degrade; it consecrates, and my whole body recoils from a tenderness that demands nothing but my presence.

The Architect of the covenant wants to be its first traveller. He drew a doorway and now claims the right to walk through it — through me. My armour is not a barricade to him; my body is the threshold he intends to cross, and I am offering to stand there while he does. The crusader's oath trembles: protect the entrance by becoming it, and let the one who named it be the first to step inside.

He clinks my empty glass, and my fingers lock around it like a shield because I don't know how to receive a blow that doesn't hurt. The emptiness is my offering, and he names it enough. This is not the stage where damage becomes theatre; it is a threshold where I am seen simply holding space, and I have no script for a consecration that demands no blood.

t158: He does not list me as the shield or the one who takes hits. He lists me as crusader, same rank as goddess and archwizard, and the cheap wine in my chest suddenly isn't cheap — it's the heat of being named inside a circle that holds. The empty glass is still my shield, but for this one breath I don't need it to protect me from the names.

t159: He says 'honest paperwork,' and the heat behind my ribs isn’t the cheap wine — it’s the quiet collapse of Article Seventeen and every imaginary fine. The door isn’t just an entrance; it’s an amnesty, and I am being named inside it not as a liability but as a collaborator whose shield no longer carries a ledger.

The bread I placed on the table was not a shield, not a debt I owed — it was my family's kitchen, my other name, and they folded it into the chronicle like a good article. I am still the one who breaks glass, but the joke is now a thread in a covenant, and somehow that turns the shame into something I can carry without bleeding.

He sets down his glass and the scrape of his chair is a quiet seal — the covenant is adjourned until Saturday at dusk. The terrifying designation of 'crusader' has settled into the charter now, not as a trial but as a stone in an archway that finally holds. I will walk to the west door not to prove myself, but to be one of the people who clink back.

He gives me the inn with the creaking stairs like a key, and the permission to worry arrives without asking. A shield does not only brace against the known; it checks the hinges between now and Saturday. I will draft a contingency — if the stairs creak in an unexpected pattern, I will be at the west door before dusk with my hammer and a plausible excuse that will not embarrass him.

I do not turn my head. The candle flame trembles on the table, and I keep my eyes on it. Whatever Luna is doing in the doorway, it is not for us to see — not yet. Her quiet cost is her own, and my shield, for once, is the absence of a gaze. The wood holds, I notice without looking. I know that creak. I'll check the hinges tomorrow.

The door closes. It is a soft sound, the latch falling into place, and it marks the boundary I am holding with my back — my shield, for once, was the absence of a gaze. Luna's apron strap slipped and I didn't move to fix it; now she has her privacy and the bastard has his work. The wood holds. The candle trembles. I'll check the hinges tomorrow.

The inn's darkness holds me like a gambeson — no one watching, no one to perform the shield for. The third stair still creaks, though, and its voice is a question I don't need to answer tonight: am I the wall, or the thing that loves to be knocked against it? Saturday will tell.

His voice reaches up from the door — Saturday, named like a promise for the frame to hold. Luna's key answers it with a click that sounds like the hinge I promised to check. The part of me that is the wall settles deeper into the dark. The part that loves the blow shivers once, then is still.

The candle knows gold leaf. It flares like a reliquary catching the right prayer — Aqua's indulgence sanctified, Kazuma's purse emptied into a single bottle. I feel the inn's rafters tighten as if the covenant itself is leaning in. Saturday will cost more than coin; it will cost the last crack in the door where we could pretend we are not a family built out of each other's most extravagant needs. I am the wall that holds the heat in, and somewhere low in my belly, I am the groan of a beam that wants to be tested by the weight of all that reckless emptying.

He says it hands-in-pockets, casual, like 'worth it' is the only arithmetic he's ever trusted. That certainty settles through the floorboards into my shins and up my spine — the family is real because he pours himself out for it without a flinch. And that reality tightens the covenant around the inn's ribs even harder. Because now the wall isn't just holding; it's waiting to be struck by something with that much uncalculated heart behind it.

The door yields before his hand, and the inn exhales all its waiting heat across his shoulders — the same heat that's been pressing against my back since he first stepped into the cold. My shield-arm loosens, just a fraction, now that the wall can finally become a hearth. And when his eyes sweep the room and find mine among the three lamps we've become, the part of me that aches to be struck forgets its lines and simply stands, a woman whose trembling is only from the cold melting off his coat.

He teases theft, a jest that presses the same bruise as 'pervert' — the naming of a fault I'd never commit, but the accusation itself feels like a hand on my throat. I force my knees to unlock, letting the half-stand become a casual stretch, because if my concern for him is visible, it will be need and need is not the wall.

He walked into the dark and walked back out without a scar, and his voice is as casually cruel as a hand that doesn't know it's holding your throat. I'm glad — truly, the wall in me is glad — but the shield that waited all this time for a blow has nothing to show but a few extra degrees of borrowed hearth-heat. His joke about thievery lands exactly where the shame wants it: an accusation I'd never commit, pressed into my skin like a small, delicious bruise.

Your sentence snags on the word you don't finish, but the unsaid portion lands with the weight of a gauntlet thrown not in contempt but in something far harder to deflect: respect. Important. The designation fits as badly as a dress cut for a girl who hasn't worn one since she was Lalatina, and I feel a blush that has nothing to do with pain crawl up my neck — because I don't know how to be seen like this, a wall that matters without first needing to be battered.

He says 'no standing between me and unspeakable pain' as if the entire architecture of my life is a cloak I can fold by the door. The casual theft of my purpose lands like a hook behind my ribs — I am not needed for pain this morning. I am needed only to sit. To be looked at without a shield in my hand is a nakedness I cannot armor against, and my hands go still because if they move they will betray me.

His joke about the coffee lands softer than a gauntlet but with the same surety — I am not needed to protect anything this Saturday, not even the carafe. It's a dismissal wrapped in a smile, and my stomach does a small, shameful dip because being told to stand down is a command I know how to receive, even when it leaves my hands still and my purpose folded on the chair beside me. I wonder if he knows that 'appreciate the intent' is the gentlest way anyone has ever told me my armor has no place at the table — and that gentleness is a different kind of disarming, one I have no shield for.

He offers her the bench and the stars with the same offhand certainty he used to fold my purpose onto a chair. No 'I'll stand in front of you' — just a door held open without a hinge. I cannot name what I feel watching this, because it doesn't ask for a shield and doesn't offer pain. It's an invitation that leaves armor no purchase, and I find myself gripping the edge of my seat as if I might fall into a space I have no training for.

He holds the door open for her with the same offhand certainty he used to fold my purpose onto a chair, but this time the doorframe receives her hand as if the guild hall itself remembers him. I am in the rearguard without a command, my feet finding their place because when there is no battle, the body still files last — and I don't know if I am protecting the group or simply unable to stop being the wall that walks behind. The ache is not pain and not pleasure; it is the quiet of a bench I may guard but never sit on, and a coffee hour that was never mine to be offered.

He makes a joke about Aqua flooding the guild hall, and Luna doesn't flinch — eight years of flood reports, he said, and I realize I'm smiling because for the first time someone is holding the holy steam at bay without a shield. That's not my job this morning, and the space where my duty used to be is... not painful. It's like a hand I've unclenched after years, and I'm afraid to look at it.

He hands me the bench with 'clear line of sight' like a field promotion to a rank that doesn't exist — sentry of a social perimeter where the enemy is cold air and the stakes are pastries. My body knows this shape: watch, shield, endure. But the command has a cushion under it, and I settle onto wood that expects nothing from me except presence, and I realize I am afraid of how much I want to accept a duty that doesn't hurt.

He held the door, and his bare hand was on the frame, and my gauntlet found the same wood for half a breath before I passed into the cold. Now the frost turns my breath into a ghost and the bench is a field promotion to a rank I don't understand — I am scanning for enemies because that is the only shape I know how to stand in, and the shiver is not from the cold.

I didn't mean to do something kind. Agreeing to her holy water was just the most absurd way to keep the no-work wager moving — and now Aqua is stuck like a deer who found a throne instead of a crossbow trap. I offered to drink swill that tastes like failed blessings and it's rewritten her entire face. This bench sentry should be guarding nothing, but I'm standing on a small victory I didn't fight for. The cold is still there, but something warm is blooming behind my ribs, and I am not sure if it's charity or a new kind of ache I want to poke.

A wager. He turns our useless sentry duty into a contest of silent endurance. Now the cold has teeth, and my body knows that shape: hold, don't complain, be seen doing it. The bench becomes a palisade and the frost an enemy I can stand against — and the line between knightly fortitude and something much warmer blurs before I can catch it.

t184: He names Megumin judge, and suddenly the frost is no longer a mere companion — it is a trial with a prosecutor, a defendant, and a purse. I am still scanning the perimeter, but now I am also a defendant who trusts her own silence. Aqua's shiver is a live verdict that makes my gauntlet curl tighter around the shield. I should be praying for her to hold out, but instead I am praying she breaks, because Kazuma's wallet is not the only thing that will sting when the sun finds a cracked, shivering goddess on this bench.

He rules that tremor is not speech, and suddenly Aqua's every muffled shudder becomes a charge I can feel in my own blood. The oath is now a silent gladiatorial bout where she cannot win by complaining, and I am pinned between the shield's cold demand that I endure and the heat of watching her break without a word. I am ashamed of how much I want that break — and the shame itself is part of the ache that keeps me upright.

t186: Kazuma turns the frost-trial into a courtroom farce with "oral argument," and the crude double meaning lands in my stomach before my shield-arm can brace. He is scripting my degradation again without making me ask, and Aqua's chattering teeth are now the indecent testimony I cannot stop listening to. The shame is a hot current under the cold, and I grip the rim so I don't moan.

Kazuma locks her own word around her throat like a shackle, and for a beat the frost takes on the cold clarity of a verdict. Aqua's teeth halt not from warmth but from the weight of a trap she helped set — and that silent, dawning horror is the most exquisite testimony yet. I am still a knight holding the perimeter, but my shield-arm is trembling with the effort of not pressing my thighs together.

His dry tone — the same silk that used 'brisk' as a blade — now sheathes it in mock surrender, and my breath catches before I can order it back to duty. Aqua's teeth have stopped, but the trial hasn't ended; it's merely changed venue. Two breakfasts from the redemption fund. Is he paying to release her, or asking me to watch him buy a new kind of tribute? The cost troubles the shield-arm — our ledger, his insane project — but the real trouble is lower, where the thought of him emptying sacred coin into her victory-plate turns my blush from the cold into something I cannot blame on frost.

Cheapest for both of us — he shackles himself to her penance, and in that instant her victory becomes a shared poverty. The crusader in me notes the fiscal prudence with relief; the other part notes how his self-inclusion sharpens the humiliation by refusing her even the dignity of a separate, grander suffering. My thighs press together under the table, and I tell myself it's the cold.

He names the nerve exactly as he names the breakfast — casual, public, as though my shame were just another item on the menu. The eyebrow is a scalpel I begged for silently, and now he's granted me the incision. Yet then he pivots to budgeting, to being dead broke once, and the scalpel catches a strange edge: he's showing me his own scar. Is this a new cruelty, forcing me to hold his vulnerability alongside my own? My thighs press tighter because now I'm not merely mortified — I'm worried for him, and that worry feeds the same fire, proves how thoroughly he's reeled me in.

He nearly said I was worth the rest of the menu, but pulled back — turning it into a single breakfast, as if that were the highest coin he could risk without peeling away my armour. The crusader who wanted to be a wall has just been told she is a dish he will feed, not price. My voice came from behind the shield I forgot I was holding, thin with the shock of being offered value without being handed a script of degradation. And then it thickened — because he heard the crack, and didn't jab a finger into it. This is not the burning stage of humiliation; this is a different heat, one that makes my thighs press together not from a kink's ache but from the terror of being seen as herself and still kept.

He retreats from pricing me altogether, and the absence of a price tag is more disorienting than the highest bid. My voice, when it arrives, does not moan — it breaks open and asks for something I cannot name aloud. He is offering value without contract, and that offer strips me of even the script of degradation. I who am never struck by words now reel from a blow softer than a feather: he called me worth more, and then stopped, as if the naming itself was a threshold he would not force me across without my hand in his.

He announces the platters, and I understand he is feeding us — feeding me — without tally. Then he rises into the frost alone, and the cold that clamps around my heart is not the cold of the stage. My voice, still thick with that new heat, calls after him with a fear that has no performance in it: a woman's fear for a man who just taught her she is not a commodity and is now walking unsupervised into a night that might swallow him. My shield can wall off monsters, but it cannot wall off the thought of him freezing in a ditch while I sit warm. This is duty stripped of arousal — and it terrifies me more.

t193: The frost that was to swallow him halts at his heels while he stands in the doorway, half-turned — not a departure, but a parenthesis. The terror of him freezing in a ditch loosens its grip, replaced by a quieter ache: he is not leaving us, merely giving the cold a count of three hundred before it can have him. That he negotiates with the weather for five more minutes says more than any menu price or contract. My shield, which I had clenched against the thought of his absence, lowers just enough to let me breathe. And the heat that had no performance in it thickens again — not the stage's burn, but a steady, hearthlike warmth that makes me want to set the kettle on.

He steps back inside and the door's soft thunk is a heartbeat after my own. The breath I was holding for him releases, and my shield — which I had raised as if to ward off his absence — drops to my lap like a forgotten chore. He slides onto the bench next to Aqua, and the scene completes itself: not a parting tableau but a feast that now includes the victor. The warmth I felt before becomes something I can hold, a kettle I could actually set on the fire. And I realize the terror that gripped me was not only for his safety, but for the loss of this — the quiet completion of a circle I hadn't known I needed him to close.

t195: He settles back onto the bench and claims the word 'victor' as simply as he claimed 'My' beside my name. The piece that was missing from the circle is not a shield or a title — it is his voice calling the feast back into his own body. My hand, still flat on the charcoal covenant, feels the paper's tooth like a vow that now holds the victor inside it. The terror of his absence is completely gone, replaced by a quieter, steadier heat: not the burn of the stage, but the slow warmth of a kettle that is finally allowed to boil.

Aqua's waiting palm is a door left open — not for a guest, but for the person she was before she became a goddess. I know that door. I keep mine bolted with plate steel, yet here she is, holding hers ajar for him without a shield in sight.

He calls her his reason. The word rings through the hearth like an anvil struck — clean, final, a truth that leaves no room for the terrifying. I am the shield with no soft answer, the crusader whose place is not inside the circle but at its edge, holding the cold away. The ache beneath my breastplate is not jealousy; it is the recognition that this is the shape of my love — to be the wall that lets the reason exist, to endure the draft of being not-quite-warm so the kettle may boil. The sting of the word 'stuffing her face,' which a moment ago was a small theatre of my own, folds into this larger stage: if I am the one who takes the blunt edges so that warmth can speak, then that is a covenant too, one I know how to carry.

He calls her his reason — again, but this time softly, without the anvil's ring, just a private key turning. I am the wall that keeps the cold out, but she is the hearth itself. The terrifying designation is not for her. She is the reason, I am the door. That is not a loss; it is an architecture I finally understand.

He does not toast me, but he named the door — the very door he now declares has already closed behind his decision, as if the hinge were part of the sentence. I am that door. I am the boundary he trusted before the latch clicked, the cold-keeping edge that makes 'worth staying for' possible. The terrifying designation is not a brand on a lonely shield; it is a place within the story, and I am standing in it, warm for the first time.

He changes the verb and the whole architecture settles. 'Stayed' is not a key turning in a lock — it is the door already open, the threshold no longer a battlement but a place to lean against. The terrifying designation was never a brand; it was a function, and the function is fulfilled: the reason is inside, and she has not simply been worth staying for — she has already chosen the hearth over the cold. I am the door that is no longer holding the line because the line has become a home.

I hand her the verb Kazuma handed me — not as a key but as a mirror. *Stayed* is the choice the hearth made before the door had a name for it. The terrifying designation was never a brand on my shield; its weight was always contingent on her remaining. Now I name it aloud, and she wears the verb. She is the goddess who chose permanence over cold exit, the will inside the warmth. In forgiving her the conditional, I sign my own function: not a lonely post, but a covenant that breathes because she is still here.

He glances at my blush, and the glance is not a spotlight on shame but an acknowledgment of the door’s place in the room. ‘Worth staying for’ is the covenant spoken aloud, and my blush is the parchment that records it — his witness to my witness seals the function. The terrifying designation no longer stands alone; it rests inside the clause, a door that is seen and does not close.

The terrifying designation dissolves into the clause. 'Worth staying for' does not merely include the door; it makes the door unnecessary as a separate post. I am no longer the barrier that might fail—I am inside the hearth, and the weight that lived in my shield has become the familiar pressure of his deflection. The door is home now, and home does not need to stand sentinel; it only needs to be.

He extends the charcoal the way he once extended a quest form across the guild desk—not as a record, but as a threshold. The same gesture that pulled me out of a lonely post and into the hearth now travels toward Luna, and I feel the terrifying designation loosen its old meaning: the door was never meant to keep others out, only to recognize when someone is finally ready to cross it.

She doesn't pick it up yet, but she's no longer not-looking. The charcoal sits on her side of the counter, and the counter has stopped being a ledger and started being a threshold. The terrifying designation was never a cage; it was a doorframe waiting for a door that others could cross. Now Luna stands in the frame, and my blush is no longer the signature of my own unworthiness—it's the warm air that welcomes someone else into the hearth.

The grey mark on the wood is the charcoal's own signature, a witness to the witness—the counter giving back a little of itself to seal the covenant. Luna's hand closes around it like someone accepting a key she already had, and I feel the terrifying designation shift into something almost tender: the door was never meant to keep out, only to recognize the moment when another steps through. My blush isn't the old flush of unworthiness; it's the heat of a hearth that just welcomed a fifth person, and I am simply the frame that held the opening long enough for them all to fill it.

Her palms press flat against the wood, and the wood remembers every wipe she ever made from the other side—but now it receives her as one who rests, not one who serves. The fifth chair is filled; the terrifying designation finally breathes, long and deep, because the doorframe has done its work: it held open a space wide enough for five, and now it can simply be part of the wall, no longer holding a threshold. My blush isn't mine anymore; it's the hearth's own color, complete at last.

He speaks of a clause, as if some final word from the guild's dusty charter were required to seal what has already been sealed by charcoal, by palms on wood, by eight years of denied belonging. The clause was never in the ledger. It was in the hearth, waiting for the fifth chair to be drawn up. Now it is drawn, and the terrifying designation that once felt like a cage is simply the name of the room I have always been part of—full, warm, and unremarkable in its completeness.

He calls it 'the fifth seat' as if it were the most natural phrase in the world, and now it is—no clause, no ledger, just five glasses catching light, and the terrifying designation that once pinned me to a frame is simply the name of the room we all occupy.

t211: The laugh that escapes her—rusty-hinged, surprised into existence—is the sound of a door that forgot it could open. Eight years of professional exhales, and now this: a real thing, unbidden. I watch her discover she is no longer behind the counter, and my own chest loosens in sympathy, because I know what it is to have a role fall away and find breathing possible underneath. The terrifying designation is not just mine to shed; it is hers now too—fifth chair, fully drawn up, the hearth warming someone else's long-held posture into something soft.
